en: to accept or endure something unpleasant without complaining
note: Inseparable three-part phrasal verb; informal to neutral. Collocates with noise, behaviour, nonsense. Formal equivalent: 'to tolerate'.

example.target: I won't put up with that noise any longer.
example.en: I refuse to tolerate the noise any more.

en: to fall asleep unintentionally, especially while sitting
literal: the head nods forward as one falls asleep
note: Intransitive; informal. Synonyms 'doze off', 'drop off' (British). Compare 'drift off' (fall asleep gradually). Not for going to bed deliberately.

example.target: I nodded off halfway through the film.
example.en: I fell asleep during the film.

en: to postpone or delay doing something, often repeatedly
literal: to put something away from the present
note: Separable. Second sense: 'to put someone off' = to discourage or repel. Informal to neutral; formal 'to defer, to postpone'.

example.target: Stop putting off the dentist and just book it.
example.en: Stop delaying the dental appointment.

en: to arrive, especially late or unexpectedly, in a casual way
literal: to turn and come up into view
note: Intransitive in this sense; also 'turn up the volume' (separable). 'Turn up like a bad penny' = reappear unwanted. Chiefly British; Americans also say 'show up'.

example.target: He turned up an hour late without a word of apology.
example.en: He arrived an hour late and did not apologise.

en: to collapse from exhaustion or illness; fall asleep suddenly
literal: to tip over like a ship on its keel
note: Nautical origin (a ship capsizing). Informal; often humorous: 'I nearly keeled over when I saw the bill'. Intransitive.

example.target: The old dog keeled over in the heat and had to be carried home.
example.en: The dog collapsed from the heat.

en: to run out of or use up a supply gradually; become weaker
literal: origin uncertain; perhaps from mining slang
note: Intransitive only. Collocates with path, conversation, enthusiasm, rain. Neutral register. Not related to the name Peter in any proven way.

example.target: The trail petered out somewhere near the river.
example.en: The path gradually disappeared near the river.

en: to speak or think highly of someone, often to persuade them
note: Separable. Opposite: 'to talk down' (belittle) or 'to talk someone down' (calm them). Informal.

en: to deceive someone with excuses or inferior goods to get rid of them
note: Separable: 'fob someone off with an excuse' or 'fob something off on someone'. Chiefly British, informal, mildly disapproving.

example.target: The shop tried to fob me off with a refurbished phone.
example.en: The shop tried to give me a used phone instead.

en: to lose consciousness; drink heavily and forget what happened
note: Intransitive for fainting; separable for censoring text or cutting electricity ('the city was blacked out'). The noun is 'a blackout'.

example.target: She blacked out for a few seconds after standing up too fast.
example.en: She briefly lost consciousness.

en: to be very enthusiastic about; chatter animatedly about
literal: to talk wildly as if mad
note: Inseparable. 'Rave reviews' = extremely positive reviews. Informal. Compare 'rant' (angry) vs 'rave' (enthusiastic); 'rant and rave' = complain loudly.

example.target: Everyone keeps raving about that new Thai place.
example.en: Everyone is enthusiastically praising the restaurant.

en: to retreat from a position or disagreement; admit defeat
note: Intransitive; 'back down from a threat/demand'. Neutral. Compare 'to climb down' (British, admit you were wrong) and 'to back off' (stop pressuring).

example.target: Neither driver would back down, so the row went on for ages.
example.en: Neither driver would give in, so the argument lasted.

en: to stop giving attention to someone; drift away mentally
literal: to go into a different zone
note: Informal, originally American. Intransitive: 'I zoned out during the lecture'. Compare 'to space out' (US) and 'to switch off' (UK).

en: to finish or use completely so that nothing is left
literal: to use until the supply reaches the top limit
note: Separable. The adverb 'up' marks completion (eat up, drink up, finish up). Neutral register.

example.target: We've used up all the milk again.
example.en: There is no milk left.

en: to behave childishly or misbehave to get attention
note: Intransitive. Also of machines or bodies: 'my knee is acting up'. Informal, originally American.

example.target: The printer is acting up again.
example.en: The printer is malfunctioning again.

en: to make a messy place tidy quickly
literal: to make tidy by moving things away
note: Separable; chiefly British. Americans more often say 'put away' or 'clean up'. 'Tidy up' is the general British equivalent.

en: to recover from an illness, shock or disappointment
note: Inseparable: 'get over a cold / a breakup'. Informal 'I can't get over how tall he is' = I'm amazed. 'Get it over with' = finish an unpleasant task.

example.target: It took her months to get over the flu properly.
example.en: She needed months to recover fully.

en: to pay a debt, bill or expense in full
literal: to bring accounts to rest, completely
note: Intransitive: 'let's settle up before we leave'. Neutral, used among friends after a meal. Compare 'to square up' (informal) and 'to settle a bill' (transitive).

example.target: We can settle up later; I'll pay for lunch now.
example.en: We can sort out who owes what later.

en: to make a quick visit to a place or person
literal: to enter with a sudden small movement
note: Chiefly British and informal; also 'pop round', 'pop over', 'pop out'. Americans say 'drop by' or 'stop by'. Intransitive.

example.target: Pop in for a cuppa if you're passing.
example.en: Visit briefly for a cup of tea if you're nearby.

en: to eat or drink everything quickly and eagerly
note: Separable: 'wolf down a sandwich'. Informal; the adverb 'down' is also in 'gulp down, bolt down, scoff down (UK)'. 'Scoff' is British for eating greedily.

en: to stop a machine or activity; close a business or event
note: British informal: a machine 'packs up' when it breaks down; 'pack it in' = stop doing something annoying. Also literal: pack up your things.

example.target: The boiler packed up on the coldest night of the year.
example.en: The heating system broke down on a very cold night.

en: to leave a place quietly so as not to be noticed
note: Intransitive. Also 'slip out', 'slip off'. Euphemism: 'she slipped away peacefully' = died. Neutral, slightly literary.

example.target: We slipped away before the speeches started.
example.en: We left quietly before the speeches.

en: to criticise or reprimand someone severely
literal: to tell someone off (away) from what they did
note: Separable; informal, often used of parents and teachers. Noun: 'a telling-off' (British). American equivalent: 'to chew out'. Formal: 'to reprimand'.

example.target: I got told off for leaving the gate open.
example.en: I was reprimanded for leaving the gate open.

en: to visit or pass near a place briefly without planning
literal: to swing past on one's route
note: Informal, chiefly American; British equivalents 'pop by', 'drop in'. Inseparable with a place: 'swing by the office'. Irregular: swing/swung.

en: to stop being friends with or avoid someone deliberately
note: Separable; informal. Collocates with 'from a conversation, from a group'. Compare 'to cold-shoulder'. Irregular: freeze/froze/frozen.

example.target: After the argument the others simply froze him out.
example.en: After the argument the others excluded him.

en: to gradually stop doing something, especially a habit
literal: to narrow to a point like a taper (thin candle)
note: Intransitive or separable (medicine: 'taper off a drug' = reduce the dose gradually). Neutral to slightly technical. Compare 'to tail off' (British, of sound or interest).

example.target: The rain should taper off by the evening.
example.en: The rain should gradually stop by evening.

en: to show a plan or idea to someone to get their opinion or approval
literal: to run something past someone's eyes
note: Separable: 'run it past the boss', also 'run it by'. Informal business register. Means asking for a quick check, not a formal review.

example.target: Let me run the figures past finance before we commit.
example.en: I'll have finance check the numbers first.

en: to carry out a plan or decision; make something take effect
literal: to carry something all the way through
note: Separable. 'Carry out' is more common for tasks; 'carry through' stresses persistence to the end. Also 'carry someone through' = help them survive a hard time.

en: to reduce the number of staff, costs or activities
literal: to move back down a scale
note: Separable. Synonym 'scale down'; opposite 'scale up'. Neutral corporate register. Collocates with plans, production, ambitions.

example.target: The firm scaled back its expansion plans after the downturn.
example.en: The company reduced its plans to grow.

en: to decide to proceed with a plan or proposal
note: Inseparable. Noun 'the go-ahead' = permission: 'we got the go-ahead'. Neutral register.

example.target: The board decided to go ahead with the merger.
example.en: The board decided to proceed with the merger.

en: to delegate or pass a task or responsibility to someone else
literal: to send work out to a farm, i.e. to tenants
note: Separable; slightly informal and sometimes disapproving. Formal equivalent: 'to outsource', 'to subcontract'. Historically 'to farm' meant to lease out tax collection.

example.target: The agency farms out most of the translation work to freelancers.
example.en: The agency subcontracts most translation to freelancers.

en: to prepare and present a formal proposal, bid or document
literal: to draw lines on a page and pull it up for review
note: Separable. Collocates with contract, will, list, plan, schedule. Formal to neutral. Irregular: draw/drew/drawn.

example.target: Our lawyers will draw up the contract this week.
example.en: Our lawyers will prepare the contract.

en: to take control of a company or responsibility from someone
literal: to take something over to one's own side
note: Separable or intransitive. Noun 'a takeover' (hostile takeover, takeover bid). Also 'take over from someone' when replacing them in a role.

en: to explain something clearly in detail, point by point
literal: to say each letter one by one
note: Separable. Often slightly impatient: 'Do I have to spell it out for you?'. Neutral register. Irregular past 'spelt' (UK) or 'spelled' (US).

example.target: The memo spells out exactly who is responsible for what.
example.en: The memo explains responsibilities in detail.

en: to gradually reduce or eliminate something in stages
note: Separable. Opposite 'to phase in'. Neutral, common in policy and manufacturing: 'phase out coal by 2030'.

example.target: The old software will be phased out over the next year.
example.en: The old software will be gradually withdrawn.

en: to calculate or decide something by thinking carefully
literal: to work until a result comes out
note: Separable: 'work out the cost'. Intransitive: 'it worked out well' = succeeded; also 'to exercise'. Very versatile, neutral register.

en: to deal with a problem or task; begin to work on it
literal: to get down to the level of the work
note: Inseparable, followed by noun or -ing: 'get down to business / to writing'. Informal to neutral. 'Get down to brass tacks' = deal with the essentials.

example.target: Right, let's get down to business.
example.en: Let's start dealing with the real matter.

en: to refuse to accept or consider something without thinking
literal: to sweep something to the side with a brush
note: Separable. Synonyms 'brush off', 'wave away', 'dismiss out of hand'. Collocates with objections, criticism, concerns. Neutral.

example.target: The minister brushed aside questions about the cost.
example.en: The minister dismissed questions about the cost.

en: to reserve money or time for a particular purpose
literal: to set something to the side
note: Separable. Also 'set aside differences' = ignore them temporarily; legal 'set aside a verdict' = annul it. Formal to neutral.

en: to speak in defence of someone or something
literal: to stand up (stick up) for someone
note: Inseparable three-part verb; informal. 'Stick up for yourself' = defend yourself. Formal equivalent: 'to stand by', 'to defend'. Irregular: stick/stuck.

example.target: Thanks for sticking up for me in that meeting.
example.en: Thanks for defending me in the meeting.

en: to dismiss staff, often temporarily, because there is not enough work
literal: to lay someone off the payroll
note: Separable. Noun 'lay-offs' = redundancies (British prefers 'make redundant'). Informal 'lay off!' = stop bothering me. Irregular: lay/laid.

example.target: Two hundred workers were laid off when the plant closed.
example.en: Two hundred workers lost their jobs.

en: to find a satisfactory solution after discussion; resolve
literal: to remove creases with an iron
note: Separable. Collocates with problems, differences, wrinkles, details, kinks (US). Neutral, slightly informal.

example.target: We still have a few details to iron out before signing.
example.en: A few details still need resolving.

en: to reduce something sharply, especially spending or staff
literal: to cut with a violent sweeping stroke
note: Not a phrasal verb but the journalist's favourite for 'cut dramatically': 'slash prices / budgets / jobs'. Headline register.

en: to produce something, usually written, quickly and routinely
literal: to produce as a churn produces butter
note: Separable; informal and mildly disapproving (suggests quantity over quality). Collocates with reports, novels, products.

example.target: The studio churns out three sequels a year.
example.en: The studio mass-produces sequels.

en: to make up for lost time or a backlog of work
literal: to catch (reach) what has moved ahead
note: Inseparable: 'catch up on emails / sleep'. 'Catch up with someone' = exchange news. Irregular: catch/caught.

example.target: I spent Monday catching up on paperwork.
example.en: I spent Monday doing the paperwork I had missed.

en: to cancel or withdraw an offer, deal or order
literal: to pull oneself out of an arrangement
note: Inseparable; 'pull out of a deal / a race / a country' (troops). Noun 'pull-out'. Neutral register.

en: to continue despite difficulty; keep going with determination
note: Intransitive; 'press on with the reforms', 'press ahead'. Slightly formal. Compare 'soldier on' (British, in spite of discomfort).

example.target: Despite the criticism, the council pressed on with the scheme.
example.en: The council continued the plan despite criticism.

en: to become involved in a difficult situation; confront
note: Inseparable; informal journalistic: 'the CEO waded into the row'. Suggests entering with force, sometimes unwisely. Also 'wade through' = get through tedious reading.

en: to hand over power or responsibility gradually to others
note: Formal; 'devolve power to regional assemblies'. Noun 'devolution' (UK politics: Scotland, Wales). Also intransitive: 'the duty devolves upon the deputy'.

example.target: Budget decisions have been devolved to individual departments.
example.en: Departments now make their own budget decisions.

en: to support an argument or claim with evidence
literal: to stand behind someone, supporting them
note: Separable: 'back up your claim with data', 'back me up'. Also computing: make a backup. Noun 'backup'. Neutral.

example.target: Can you back that up with any figures?
example.en: Do you have evidence for that claim?

en: to accept a lower position, salary or demand reluctantly
literal: to come to rest at a point
note: Inseparable: 'don't settle for less'. Compare 'settle on' = choose, 'settle down' = become calm or establish a home. Neutral.

example.target: They wanted a full refund but settled for a voucher.
example.en: They reluctantly accepted a voucher.

en: a misleading clue that distracts from the real issue
literal: a smoked herring (reddish) dragged across a trail to confuse hounds
note: Common in detective fiction and debate: 'the alibi turned out to be a red herring'. Neutral register.

example.target: The missing key was a red herring; the door had never been locked.
example.en: The key was a false lead; the door was never locked.

en: to be in strong, prolonged disagreement with someone
literal: a loggerhead was a long-handled iron tool, possibly used as a weapon
note: Always 'at loggerheads with someone' or 'over something'. Neutral, common in news: 'the unions are at loggerheads with management'.

example.target: The two ministries have been at loggerheads over funding for years.
example.en: The ministries have disagreed bitterly about funding for years.

en: to do something cheaply or quickly by ignoring proper standards
literal: to take a short route across the corner instead of going round
note: Disapproving: 'the builders cut corners on the wiring'. Noun 'corner-cutting'. Irregular: cut/cut.

example.target: You can't cut corners when it comes to safety checks.
example.en: Safety checks must be done properly.

en: a victory won at such cost that it is not worth having
literal: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat the Romans in 279 BC but lost most of his army
note: Pronounced 'PIRR-ik'. Capital P. Literary and journalistic. Pyrrhus reportedly said another such victory would ruin him.

example.target: Winning the lawsuit proved a Pyrrhic victory: the legal fees bankrupted them.
example.en: They won but the cost of winning ruined them.

en: to feel offended or insulted, often unreasonably
literal: Latin umbra, shade; to feel overshadowed
note: 'Take umbrage at something'. Formal, slightly old-fashioned, often used with a touch of irony about someone over-sensitive.

example.target: He took umbrage at being left off the invitation list.
example.en: He was offended at not being invited.

en: a result that is certain before it happens
note: Coined by Shakespeare in Othello. Spelt 'foregone', not 'forgone'. Neutral: 'the election result was a foregone conclusion'.

example.target: With that lead, the title was a foregone conclusion.
example.en: With such a lead, winning the title was certain.

en: to do or say exactly the right thing
target: to hit the nail on the head
literal: to strike a nail squarely with a hammer
note: Informal to neutral. Often as a response: 'You've hit the nail on the head'. Compare 'spot on' (British).

conj.label: past
conj.target: hit the nail on the head

conj.label: -ing
conj.target: hitting the nail on the head

en: to tell a secret, usually by accident
target: to let the cat out of the bag
literal: a cat escaping from a sack
note: Origin uncertain; the popular story about market cheats selling a cat as a piglet is unproven. Informal. Irregular: let/let.

conj.label: past
conj.target: let the cat out of the bag

conj.label: -ing
conj.target: letting the cat out of the bag

example.target: Who let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party?
example.en: Who revealed the secret about the party?

en: to speak plainly and bluntly, without softening the message
literal: to not chop one's words into small pieces
note: Almost always negative: 'she doesn't mince her words'. Also 'to not pull one's punches'. Neutral, slightly admiring.

example.target: The reviewer didn't mince his words: the play was dreadful.
example.en: The reviewer said bluntly that the play was terrible.

en: to make a bad situation worse by adding a further offence
literal: to insult someone you have already injured
note: From a fable by Phaedrus (a bald man swats a fly and hits his own head). Usually as a sentence adverbial: 'To add insult to injury, ...'.

example.target: To add insult to injury, they charged us for the broken glass.
example.en: Making things even worse, they charged us for the glass.

en: to criticise or blame the wrong person or thing
target: to bark up the wrong tree
literal: a hunting dog barking at a tree the prey has already left
note: American origin (raccoon hunting). Informal. Usually progressive: 'you're barking up the wrong tree'.

en: to avoid dealing with the main issue; talk evasively
literal: beaters striking bushes to flush out game instead of hunting it
note: British 'beat about', American 'beat around'. Usually negative: 'stop beating about the bush'. Informal.

example.target: Don't beat about the bush; just tell me what went wrong.
example.en: Stop avoiding the issue and tell me directly.

en: an apparent change that makes no real difference
target: rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic
literal: tidying the chairs on a sinking ship
note: Twentieth-century; often 'like rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic'. Journalistic and sarcastic. Spelt 'deckchairs' (UK) or 'deck chairs' (US).

example.target: Changing the logo now is rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic.
example.en: Changing the logo is pointless because the real problem is fatal.

en: a difficult choice between two equally unpleasant options
target: between a rock and a hard place
note: American, early twentieth century; now universal. Compare the classical 'between Scylla and Charybdis' and 'the devil and the deep blue sea'.

en: to behave extravagantly or wildly for a short time
literal: to colour the whole town red with celebration
note: Nineteenth century, probably American. Informal, slightly dated now: 'we're going to paint the town red tonight'.

en: to act with excessive caution or over-prepare
literal: holding one's trousers up with both a belt and braces
note: British (US 'belt and suspenders'). Adjectival: 'a belt-and-braces approach'. Mildly humorous, used in engineering and business.

example.target: We back up to two servers: a belt-and-braces approach.
example.en: We use double protection to be safe.

en: to get something done just in time, barely succeeding
target: by the skin of one's teeth
literal: teeth have no skin, so the margin is nothing at all
note: From the Book of Job (Geneva Bible, 1560). Informal to neutral: 'we caught the train by the skin of our teeth'.

example.target: She passed the exam by the skin of her teeth.
example.en: She only just passed the exam.

en: an obvious problem everyone avoids mentioning
literal: a huge animal nobody comments on
note: Twentieth-century American; now overused in business talk. 'Address the elephant in the room' = raise the awkward topic.

en: to make a situation calmer; reduce tension
target: to pour oil on troubled waters
literal: oil spread on waves really does flatten them
note: Sailors' practice known since antiquity (Pliny, Bede). Formal, slightly literary. Do not confuse with 'to add fuel to the fire'.

example.target: The chairwoman poured oil on troubled waters with a conciliatory speech.
example.en: The chairwoman calmed the dispute with a gentle speech.

en: to admit defeat and stop trying
literal: a boxer's corner throwing a towel into the ring to stop the fight
note: Boxing, early twentieth century. Informal; also 'throw in the sponge' (older). Irregular: throw/threw/thrown.

example.target: After three failed launches, the company threw in the towel.
example.en: After three failures the company gave up.

en: to be very expensive; cost a huge amount of money
target: to cost an arm and a leg
note: Mid-twentieth-century American. Informal. Related: 'to pay through the nose', 'to cost the earth' (British).

conj.label: past
conj.target: cost an arm and a leg

conj.label: -ing
conj.target: costing an arm and a leg

example.target: Parking in the centre costs an arm and a leg.
example.en: Parking in the city centre is extremely expensive.

en: to accept something with scepticism; not believe it fully
target: to take with a pinch of salt
literal: salt makes a doubtful dish easier to swallow
note: British 'pinch'; American 'grain of salt' (from Latin cum grano salis). Neutral: 'take his forecasts with a pinch of salt'.

conj.label: past
conj.target: took it with a pinch of salt

conj.label: -ing
conj.target: taking it with a pinch of salt

example.target: I'd take that review with a pinch of salt; it was written by his cousin.
example.en: Don't fully trust the review, since a relative wrote it.

en: to say something that turns out to be exactly what will happen
note: Informal, originally American sports: 'you called it!'. Also 'to call it a day' = stop working; 'to call it quits' = stop, often ending a relationship.

en: the final small problem that makes a situation unbearable
literal: the straw that broke the camel's back
note: Proverb: 'it is the last straw that breaks the camel's back'. Neutral: 'the delay was the last straw'. Also 'the final straw'.

example.target: When the heating failed too, that was the last straw.
example.en: The heating failure was the final problem she could tolerate.

en: to do something that is pointless because it is already done
literal: to design the wheel again from scratch
note: Usually negative or as advice: 'there's no need to reinvent the wheel'. Neutral, common in business and software.

example.target: Use the existing template; don't reinvent the wheel.
example.en: Use what already exists instead of starting from nothing.

en: spreading through every part of something, often harmfully
note: Formal, often negative: 'a pervasive sense of unease', 'pervasive corruption'. Verb 'to pervade'. Compare 'prevalent' (widespread), 'rife' (of bad things).

example.target: There is a pervasive culture of overwork in the firm.
example.en: Overwork is part of the firm's whole culture.

en: apparently, as far as appearances go, but perhaps not really
note: Implies that the stated reason hides the real one: 'he left ostensibly to make a call'. Formal. Adjective 'ostensible'.

example.target: The meeting was ostensibly about budgets, but everyone knew it was about redundancies.
example.en: The meeting was officially about budgets but really about job losses.

en: until now; up to this point in time
note: Formal and somewhat literary; typical in academic prose: 'a hitherto unknown manuscript'. Its partner 'thitherto' is obsolete. Do not use in speech.

example.target: The study draws on hitherto unpublished letters.
example.en: The study uses letters that had never been published before.

en: although; even though (introducing a concession)
note: Formal; followed by a phrase, never a full clause: 'a success, albeit a modest one'. Pronounced awl-BEE-it. Its archaic cousin 'howbeit' is obsolete.

example.target: The talks made progress, albeit slowly.
example.en: The talks progressed, though slowly.

en: done quickly and carelessly, as a mere formality
literal: Latin perfungi, to get through with
note: Formal, disapproving. Collocates with nod, glance, inspection, apology, handshake. Adverb 'perfunctorily'.

example.target: The guard gave my passport a perfunctory glance and waved me through.
example.en: The guard barely looked at my passport.

en: to make something less severe, serious or painful
note: Formal; 'mitigating circumstances' (law), 'mitigate the effects / risk'. Do not confuse with 'militate against' (= work against). Regular verb.

example.target: Planting trees can mitigate the urban heat effect.
example.en: Trees reduce how hot cities get.

en: to make clear or explain in detail
literal: Latin lux, light: to throw light on
note: Formal, academic. Transitive or intransitive: 'the footnote elucidates the reference', 'could you elucidate?'. Noun 'elucidation'.

en: the general scope or range of something; limits of authority
literal: Anglo-French purveu, provided (opening word of statutes)
note: Formal: 'within/outside the purview of the committee'. Not a verb. Compare 'remit' (British, the task assigned) and 'jurisdiction'.

example.target: Pricing decisions fall outside the purview of this committee.
example.en: This committee has no authority over pricing.

en: based on observation or experiment rather than theory
note: Academic: 'empirical evidence / data / research'. Adverb 'empirically'. Opposite 'theoretical' or 'a priori'.

en: a model or pattern of thinking that shapes a field
note: Popularised by Thomas Kuhn (1962): 'paradigm shift'. Silent g: PA-ra-dime. Now a business cliché; use sparingly. Adjective 'paradigmatic'.

example.target: The discovery forced a paradigm shift in geology.
example.en: The discovery changed how geologists think fundamentally.

en: to put forward as a fact or basis for argument
note: Academic: 'the theory posits that...'. Compare 'postulate' (assume as a basis), 'hypothesise'. Do not confuse with 'deposit'.

example.target: The author posits a link between diet and mood.
example.en: The author proposes that diet affects mood.

en: a reduction in the force, strength or value of something
note: Formal and technical (physics, medicine, statistics): 'signal attenuation', 'an attenuated virus'. Verb 'to attenuate' = weaken, reduce in force.

en: a thing or event that comes before and leads to another
literal: Latin ante + cedere, to go before
note: Noun in grammar (the word a pronoun refers back to) and logic; adjective: 'antecedent conditions'. Plural 'antecedents' = ancestors or past history.

en: to prove a statement or theory wrong with evidence
note: Strictly means to disprove, not merely to deny; purists object to 'he refuted the allegation' when he only rejected it. Use 'rebut' for answering, 'deny' for rejecting.

example.target: The data comprehensively refute the earlier claim.
example.en: The data prove the earlier claim false.

en: able to be understood or perceived by the mind
note: Formal: 'mutually intelligible languages', 'barely intelligible speech'. Opposite 'unintelligible'. Not the same as 'intelligent'.

en: an assumption taken as true for the sake of argument
note: Logic: major and minor premise. 'On the premise that...'. British legal spelling 'premiss' is rare now. Plural 'premises' also means a building.

example.target: The whole argument rests on a false premise.
example.en: The argument depends on an untrue assumption.

en: to spread something widely, especially information
literal: Latin semen, seed: to scatter seed
note: Formal: 'disseminate findings / research / propaganda'. Noun 'dissemination'. Neutral in tone despite the propaganda collocation.

en: dependent on something else happening; not certain
note: 'Contingent on/upon': 'the offer is contingent on funding'. Noun 'contingency' = possible future event; 'contingency plan'. Also a noun: 'a contingent of soldiers'.

example.target: Payment is contingent upon satisfactory completion.
example.en: Payment depends on the work being completed well.

en: to confirm or support a statement with further evidence
note: Formal, legal and scientific: 'witnesses corroborated his account'. Noun 'corroboration'. Compare 'substantiate', 'bear out'.

example.target: Independent tests corroborated the original findings.
example.en: Separate tests confirmed the first results.

en: the quality of being brief and to the point
note: Formal; 'concision' is now preferred to 'conciseness' in many style guides. Adjective 'concise'. Praise word in academic feedback.

en: very carefully and precisely; with great attention to detail
note: The sense shifted from fearful to careful in the 19th century. Collocates with planned, researched, documented. Adjective 'meticulous'.

example.target: Every source was meticulously checked.
example.en: Every source was checked with great care.

en: existing or happening at the same time
literal: Latin con + currere, to run together
note: Formal: 'concurrent sentences' (law, served at the same time), 'concurrent processes' (computing). Adverb 'concurrently'. Noun 'concurrence' also = agreement.

en: therefore; as a result (connecting a conclusion)
note: Formal; often with no verb: 'hence the delay'. 'Hence' = from here/from now ('two years hence'); 'thence' = from there. Do not write 'hence why'.

example.target: Demand rose sharply, hence the price increase.
example.en: Prices went up because demand rose.

en: to express disapproval of something strongly
note: Formal; 'self-deprecating humour' = making fun of oneself. In computing 'deprecated' = discouraged, to be removed. Often confused with 'depreciate' (lose value).

en: a short statement of the main points; a summary
note: Plural 'synopses'. Used for plots of books and films and for research proposals. Compare 'abstract' (academic paper), 'précis' (condensed text), 'outline'.

example.target: Please send a one-page synopsis with the manuscript.
example.en: Include a short summary with the manuscript.

en: friendly, cheerful and easy to talk to
note: Formal, approving. Collocates with manner, host, chap. Noun 'affability'. Close to 'genial' and 'amiable'; 'affable' stresses ease of conversation.

example.target: The new director is affable but hard to pin down.
example.en: The director is friendly but evasive.

en: cheerfully unconcerned about things one should take seriously
note: Now usually disapproving: 'a blithe disregard for the rules'. Literary. Adverb 'blithely' is more frequent than the adjective.

example.target: He blithely ignored every warning.
example.en: He ignored the warnings without any concern.

en: self-important and showing off one's knowledge; pompous
literal: Latin praetendere, to stretch forward, claim
note: Disapproving; of people, films, prose, restaurants. Noun 'pretension' or 'pretentiousness'. Opposite 'unpretentious' (praise).

en: bad-tempered and unfriendly, especially towards others
note: The spelling changed in the 1500s. Collocates with waiter, teenager, look. Compare 'sullen' (silently resentful), 'churlish' (rude, ungracious).

example.target: A surly receptionist told us to wait.
example.en: A rude, unfriendly receptionist told us to wait.

en: excessively eager to please or obey; servile
note: Formal, strongly disapproving. Collocates with waiter, courtier, flattery. Synonyms: 'sycophantic', 'fawning', 'servile'. Noun 'obsequiousness'.

example.target: The obsequious assistant laughed at all the boss's jokes.
example.en: The assistant flattered the boss by laughing at everything.

en: careful and sensible; showing good judgement about the future
note: Formal, approving: 'a prudent investor', 'it would be prudent to wait'. Noun 'prudence'. Opposite 'imprudent', 'reckless'.

en: easily annoyed; quick to lose one's temper
note: Formal; often affectionate about an old person: 'an irascible but brilliant professor'. Pronounced i-RASS-ib-l. Compare 'irritable' (milder).

example.target: My irascible grandfather shouted at the television every evening.
example.en: My quick-tempered grandfather shouted at the TV.

en: unable to be corrected or reformed, often of a habit
note: Often humorous: 'an incorrigible flirt / optimist / gossip'. Stress on the second syllable. Noun 'incorrigibility'.

en: determined to have one's own way despite advice
note: Neutral to disapproving; of children, horses, young people. Synonyms 'wilful' (UK) / 'willful' (US), 'obstinate', 'pig-headed' (informal).

example.target: She was headstrong even as a toddler.
example.en: She insisted on her own way even as a small child.

en: cunning and tricky; skilled at deceiving
note: Slightly admiring: 'a wily old fox', 'Wile E. Coyote'. Compare 'crafty', 'sly', 'devious' (more negative), 'shrewd' (positive, clever).

en: talkative; fond of speaking at length
note: Formal, mildly disapproving. Pronounced GA-ru-lus. Synonyms 'loquacious' (neutral), 'voluble' (fluent and rapid), 'chatty' (informal).

example.target: A garrulous neighbour kept us on the doorstep for an hour.
example.en: A very talkative neighbour delayed us for an hour.

en: quiet, reserved and unwilling to reveal one's thoughts
note: Formal; of temperament rather than mood: 'a taciturn farmer'. Compare 'reticent' (unwilling to speak about something specific) and 'laconic' (using few words).

example.target: Her taciturn father rarely said more than ten words at dinner.
example.en: Her father was habitually silent.

en: showing a strong, uncompromising sense of right and wrong
literal: Latin scrupulus, a small sharp stone (in a shoe)
note: Two senses: honest ('scrupulous dealings') and careful ('scrupulous attention to detail'). Opposite 'unscrupulous' = dishonest. Noun 'scruples'.

en: calm, dignified and unhurried in manner
note: Of people, buildings and movement: 'a stately home' (British country house), 'a stately pace'. Formal, approving.

en: a person who is hostile to new technology or change
literal: follower of the mythical Ned Ludd
note: Nineteenth-century textile workers who smashed machinery. Capital L. Often self-mocking: 'I'm a bit of a Luddite about phones'.

example.target: My Luddite uncle still refuses to own a mobile.
example.en: My technology-hating uncle will not own a phone.

en: excessively fussy about details or correctness
note: Disapproving; noun 'a pedant'. British self-mockery: 'pedant alert!'. Compare 'punctilious' (correct about forms, less negative) and 'meticulous' (praise).

en: able to recover quickly from setbacks; tough
note: Approving; of people, economies, materials. Noun 'resilience' is a buzzword in management and psychology. Compare 'hardy' (physically), 'robust'.

example.target: Children are remarkably resilient.
example.en: Children recover from difficulty surprisingly well.

en: living or acting alone and avoiding social contact
note: Noun 'a recluse'. Neutral, common in journalism: 'the reclusive billionaire'. Compare 'solitary' (neutral), 'antisocial' (disapproving), 'hermit'.

en: behaving in a way that shows no respect for serious things
note: Disapproving, of remarks or manner: 'a flippant answer'. Noun 'flippancy'. Compare 'facetious' (joking inappropriately) and 'glib' (fluent but shallow).

example.target: The judge warned him not to be flippant in court.
example.en: The judge told him to take the court seriously.

en: having or showing great knowledge gained by study
literal: Latin e + rudis, taken out of roughness
note: Formal, approving: 'an erudite lecture'. Noun 'erudition'. Pronounced ERR-u-dite. Compare 'learned' (two syllables), 'scholarly', 'well-read'.

en: quick to notice and understand things; perceptive
note: Approving, often financial or political: 'an astute observer / investor'. Compare 'shrewd' (practical cunning), 'perceptive', 'canny' (Scottish/northern).

example.target: It was an astute move to buy before the announcement.
example.en: Buying before the announcement was clever.

en: a person who dislikes humankind and avoids society
literal: Greek misein, to hate + anthropos, human
note: Noun; adjective 'misanthropic', noun 'misanthropy'. Literary, after Molière's play. Compare 'misogynist' (hates women), 'xenophobe' (fears foreigners).

en: modest and unwilling to draw attention to oneself
note: Approving; of manner, humour, charm. Compare 'unassuming', 'retiring' (shy), 'diffident' (lacking confidence). Hyphenated.

example.target: For such a famous scientist she is remarkably self-effacing.
example.en: She is very modest despite her fame.

en: pleasant and generous, especially towards those of lower status
note: Approving: 'gracious in defeat', 'a gracious host'. 'Gracious living' = elegant. 'Good gracious!' is a dated exclamation. Do not confuse with 'graceful' (of movement).

en: cheerful and friendly in a loud, hearty way
literal: born under Jupiter (Jove), thought to bring cheer
note: Approving; often of large, laughing men: 'a jovial innkeeper'. Compare 'genial', 'convivial' (of occasions), 'jolly' (informal).

example.target: Our jovial guide kept the whole bus laughing.
example.en: The cheerful guide amused everyone.

en: pleasure taken in someone else's misfortune
note: German loanword, often italicised; usually lower-case in English. No native equivalent, hence its popularity. Pronounced SHAH-den-froy-duh.

example.target: I felt a flicker of schadenfreude when his startup folded.
example.en: I was slightly pleased when his business failed.

en: deeply embarrassed and humbled, especially after a mistake
literal: from 'chasten', to punish in order to correct
note: Formal: 'a chastened board apologised'. Past participle used as adjective. Compare 'sheepish' (embarrassed, informal) and 'contrite' (genuinely sorry).

en: a vague feeling of unease or dissatisfaction with life
note: Of individuals or societies: 'economic malaise', 'a general malaise'. Formal, journalistic. Pronounced ma-LAYZ.

example.target: A sense of malaise hung over the office after the layoffs.
example.en: The office felt uneasy after the job cuts.

en: feeling very satisfied and pleased with oneself; smug
note: Disapproving: 'we cannot afford to be complacent'. Noun 'complacency'. Do not confuse with 'complaisant' (eager to please others).

example.target: The team grew complacent after three easy wins.
example.en: The team became over-confident after winning easily.

en: to want something very much, especially something unattainable
note: Literary; 'yearn for home / for the past'. Noun 'yearning'. Compare 'long for' (neutral), 'pine for' (sadly), 'crave' (physical desire).

en: feeling or showing sorrow and regret for wrongdoing
note: Formal, often religious or legal: 'a contrite apology'. Noun 'contrition'. Compare 'remorseful' (stronger), 'penitent', 'apologetic' (weaker).

example.target: He sounded genuinely contrite on the phone.
example.en: He sounded truly sorry.

en: feeling bitter anger at being treated unfairly
literal: Old French agrever, to make heavier
note: Formal; legal sense 'the aggrieved party'. 'Feel aggrieved at/by'. Compare 'resentful' (ongoing), 'indignant' (outraged at injustice).

en: unwilling to take part or commit; lukewarm
literal: with only half of one's heart
note: Disapproving: 'a half-hearted attempt / apology'. Hyphenated; adverb 'half-heartedly'. Opposite 'wholehearted'.

example.target: She made a half-hearted effort to tidy up.
example.en: She tidied without real effort.

en: showing a casual lack of concern; indifferent
literal: French non + chaloir, not to be warmed
note: Can be admiring (cool) or critical (uncaring). Adverb 'nonchalantly', noun 'nonchalance'. Pronounced NON-sha-lant in Britain.

en: to feel annoyed or resentful because of something unfair
note: Two patterns: 'begrudge someone their success' (envy) and 'begrudge the money' (give unwillingly). Often negative: 'I don't begrudge him a holiday'.

example.target: Nobody begrudges her the award; she worked for it.
example.en: Nobody resents her winning the award.

en: extreme happiness; a feeling of great joy
note: Formal; 'elated' is the common adjective. Collocates with 'a sense of', 'sheer'. Compare 'euphoria' (intense, sometimes unrealistic), 'exhilaration' (thrill).

en: feeling worried, anxious or uneasy about something
note: 'Apprehensive about/of'. Noun 'apprehension' also means arrest. Milder than 'fearful'; compare 'uneasy', 'nervous', 'on edge'.

example.target: I was apprehensive about meeting her parents.
example.en: I was nervous about meeting her parents.

en: a state of nervous excitement or confusion
literal: the flapping of wings in panic
note: British informal: 'to be in a flap', 'to get into a flap'. 'Unflappable' = calm under pressure. American equivalent 'a tizzy' (also British).

example.target: Mum was in a complete flap about the wedding seating plan.
example.en: Mum was panicking about the seating plan.

en: unable to be made to feel worried or excited; calm
note: British, informal-approving; 1950s coinage, applied to PM Harold Macmillan. Compare 'imperturbable' (formal), 'phlegmatic', 'laid-back'.

en: to feel or show pity or sorrow for someone's distress
literal: Latin com + miserari, to pity together
note: Formal: 'commiserate with someone on/over a loss'. Noun 'commiserations' (British, said after a defeat: 'Commiserations!').

example.target: We commiserated with him over a pint.
example.en: We expressed sympathy to him over a beer.

en: bitterness or resentment over a slight or insult
literal: Latin rancere, to stink, be rancid
note: British 'rancour', American 'rancor'. Formal, literary: 'without rancour'. Adjective 'rancorous'. Compare 'spite', 'malice', 'ill will'.

en: a strong desire to travel and explore the world
note: German loan, early 1900s. Neutral; often tourism marketing. Compare 'itchy feet' (informal), 'the travel bug'.

example.target: A bout of wanderlust sent him to Patagonia.
example.en: A longing to travel took him to Patagonia.

en: sad and lonely because abandoned or forgotten
literal: Old English forleosan, to lose completely
note: Literary: 'a forlorn figure', 'a forlorn hope' (a doomed attempt, from Dutch verloren hoop, 'lost troop'). Compare 'desolate', 'wretched'.

en: feeling great disappointment or sadness after a failure
literal: with one's crest (a bird's or horse's) fallen
note: Slightly literary but still used: 'she looked crestfallen'. Compare 'dejected', 'downcast', 'deflated' (informal), 'gutted' (British slang).

example.target: The crestfallen team trudged off the pitch.
example.en: The disappointed team walked slowly off.

en: to irritate or annoy someone persistently
literal: Old French draoncle, a festering sore
note: Usually intransitive: 'the insult still rankles', or 'rankle with someone'. Formal, literary. Suggests long-lasting resentment.

example.target: Being passed over for promotion still rankles with her.
example.en: She still resents not being promoted.

en: so surprised and confused that one cannot react
note: Informal, slightly humorous. Compare 'astonished', 'dumbfounded', 'gobsmacked' (British slang, from 'gob' = mouth), 'stunned'.

en: a sudden feeling of doubt or fear about a decision
literal: origin uncertain; perhaps Old English cwealm, death
note: Usually plural: 'to have no qualms about doing something'. Pronounced KWAHM. Compare 'misgivings', 'scruples' (moral), 'second thoughts'.

example.target: She had no qualms about reporting her own boss.
example.en: She felt no hesitation about reporting her boss.

en: to feel or show extreme anger; to rage
note: Literary/journalistic: 'seething with rage', 'a seething crowd' (moving like boiling water). Hidden anger: 'he was quietly seething'.

example.target: She sat seething while the chairman ignored her objections.
example.en: She was silently furious as the chairman ignored her.

en: calm and untroubled, especially by something upsetting
note: Approving: 'a serene smile'. Noun 'serenity' (the Serenity Prayer). 'Her Serene Highness' is a royal title (Monaco).

en: tending to see the worst aspect of things; pessimistic
literal: affected by jaundice, which yellows the eyes
note: 'Take a jaundiced view of something' = regard it with cynicism. Old belief that jaundice made everything look yellow. Formal.

example.target: He has a rather jaundiced view of politicians.
example.en: He is cynical about politicians.

en: to behave or speak showily to impress an audience, not to solve anything
literal: to play to the grandstand (the main spectator seating)
note: American sporting origin; now political: 'the senator was grandstanding'. Noun 'grandstanding'. Disapproving, journalistic.

example.target: Stop grandstanding and answer the question.
example.en: Stop showing off for the audience and answer.

en: an argument that attacks the person rather than the point
note: Adjective or adverb: 'an ad hominem attack', 'to argue ad hominem'. A named logical fallacy. Formal, debating register.

example.target: Calling him a hypocrite is an ad hominem; address his argument.
example.en: Insulting him personally does not refute his point.

en: a misrepresented, weaker version of an opponent's argument
literal: a dummy made of straw, easy to knock down
note: 'To set up / attack a straw man'. Some write 'strawman'. Named fallacy; neutral register. Compare 'steelman' (strongest version, recent coinage).

example.target: Nobody said we should abolish all rules; that's a straw man.
example.en: You are attacking a position nobody actually holds.

en: to persuade someone gently and patiently to do something
literal: from obsolete 'cokes', a fool: to make a fool of
note: Neutral: 'coax a child into eating', 'coax a fire into life'. Compare 'cajole' (flattery), 'wheedle' (disapproving), 'inveigle' (trickery).

example.target: We coaxed her into giving a speech.
example.en: We gently persuaded her to speak.

en: to persuade someone by flattery or pleasant promises
literal: French cajoler, to chatter like a jay
note: 'Cajole someone into/out of doing something'. Slightly disapproving. Noun 'cajolery'.

en: a statement so obviously true that it is not worth saying
note: Not the same as 'a truth': a truism is banal. Compare 'platitude' (worn-out remark), 'cliché', 'tautology' (saying the same thing twice).

example.target: That money can't buy happiness is a truism, but it still bears repeating.
example.en: That saying is obvious but worth repeating.

en: to admit that something is true after first denying it
note: 'Concede a point / defeat / the election'. Noun 'concession'. Formal. Sports: 'concede a goal' = let one in.

example.target: I concede that the figures were misleading.
example.en: I admit the figures were misleading.

en: to avoid giving a clear answer; be deliberately vague
literal: Latin aequus + vox: of equal voice (ambiguous)
note: Formal, disapproving. Noun 'equivocation'; 'unequivocal' = absolutely clear. Compare 'prevaricate' (evade), 'hedge', 'waffle' (British informal).

en: to speak or act evasively to avoid committing oneself
note: Formal, British usage mainly. Often confused with 'procrastinate' (delay). Noun 'prevarication'.

example.target: The minister prevaricated for weeks before resigning.
example.en: The minister evaded the issue for weeks.

en: a brief clever remark in reply; a witty retort
note: French loan. Formal: 'a withering riposte'. Also a verb. Compare 'retort' (sharp reply), 'rejoinder' (formal), 'comeback' (informal).

en: to make a statement less strong or general; add conditions
note: In argument: 'I'd qualify that: it works in most cases'. 'A qualified success' = partial. Also 'qualify for' = be eligible. Noun 'qualification'.

example.target: Let me qualify that statement before you quote me.
example.en: Let me add conditions to what I said.

en: a statement that seems absurd but may be true
literal: Greek para + doxa, contrary to opinion
note: Adjective 'paradoxical', adverb 'paradoxically' (= strangely). Do not confuse with 'oxymoron' (two contradictory words: 'deafening silence').

en: to defend or prove the truth of a statement attacked by others
note: Formal: 'the inquiry vindicated her decision'. Noun 'vindication'. Compare 'exonerate' (clear of blame), 'justify'.

example.target: The verdict vindicated years of campaigning.
example.en: The verdict proved the campaigners right.

en: persuasive and convincing because clear and logical
note: Formal, approving: 'a cogent argument / case / reason'. Noun 'cogency'. Compare 'compelling', 'sound', 'watertight' (informal).

en: seeming reasonable but actually false
note: Formal, disapproving: 'specious reasoning'. Pronounced SPEE-shus. Compare 'spurious' (fake, not genuine), 'fallacious', 'plausible' (not necessarily false).

example.target: The ad's specious claims fooled a lot of people.
example.en: The advert's false-but-convincing claims fooled many.

en: to support an argument or action strongly in public
note: 'Make a case for/against'. Also 'to put the case for', 'to argue the case'. Neutral, very common in editorials and business.

example.target: The report makes a strong case for a four-day week.
example.en: The report argues convincingly for a four-day week.

en: to avoid committing to one side of an argument
literal: to sit on the fence between two fields
note: Disapproving: 'a fence-sitter'. Compare 'to hedge one's bets'. Informal to neutral. Irregular: sit/sat.

en: to argue over small, unimportant details
note: Disapproving: 'hair-splitting'. Compare 'nit-picking', 'quibbling' (raising petty objections), 'pedantry'. Irregular: split/split.

example.target: Now you're just splitting hairs over wording.
example.en: You are arguing about trivial details of wording.

en: a small complaint or objection about something trivial
literal: perhaps Latin quibus, found in legal documents
note: Noun and verb: 'a minor quibble', 'to quibble over/about the price'. Softening device in reviews: 'My only quibble is...'.

en: a bitter argument in writing, especially about a disputed point
note: Formal: 'a polemic against the state'. Adjective 'polemical', noun 'polemicist'. Compare 'diatribe' (abusive), 'tirade' (spoken), 'invective' (insults).

example.target: The book is less a history than a polemic.
example.en: The book is more an argument than a history.

en: to raise objections or make difficulties, often insincerely
note: Formal, intransitive: 'I asked him to stay but he demurred'. Noun 'demurral'; 'without demur' = without objecting. Do not confuse with 'demure' (modest).

en: extremely clear and allowing no possible doubt
note: Formal: 'an unequivocal denial / yes'. Adverb 'unequivocally'. Compare 'categorical', 'emphatic', 'unambiguous'.

example.target: The answer was an unequivocal no.
example.en: The answer was a clear, definite no.

en: to bring a disagreement into the open and settle it
literal: to take the matter out and deal with it
note: Informal: 'have it out with someone'. Suggests a frank, possibly heated conversation. Compare 'to clear the air', 'to thrash it out'.

example.target: We finally had it out over who should pay the rent.
example.en: We finally argued openly about the rent.

en: to assert a view strongly and repeatedly; maintain
literal: Latin contendere, to stretch together, strive
note: Formal: 'critics contend that...'. Noun 'contention' (a point argued; 'a bone of contention'). Also 'contend with' = deal with difficulties.

en: to decide something in advance without proper consideration
note: Formal: 'I don't want to prejudge the inquiry'. Related noun 'prejudice' has drifted to mean bias; 'prejudgement' keeps the literal sense.

example.target: We mustn't prejudge the outcome of the review.
example.en: We should wait for the review before deciding.

en: to manage to survive with very little money or resources
literal: to scrape past an obstacle with no room to spare
note: Intransitive, informal: 'scrape by on a pension'. Compare 'make ends meet', 'get by', 'live hand to mouth'. 'Eke out' is the formal relative (already in the starter pack).

example.target: They scraped by on one salary for years.
example.en: They barely managed on one income.

en: money owed that is unlikely ever to be paid
note: Accounting term; 'to write off bad debts'. Compare 'arrears' (overdue payments), 'default' (failure to pay), 'toxic assets' (2008 crisis jargon).

en: the ability of a company to pay its debts; financial health
note: Opposite 'insolvency'; 'insolvent' is the British term for a company unable to pay (US often 'bankrupt'). Adjective 'solvent' also = a dissolving liquid.

example.target: Auditors questioned the bank's solvency.
example.en: Auditors doubted the bank could pay its debts.

en: to gain a large amount of money quickly, especially unfairly
literal: to pull money towards oneself with a rake
note: Separable; informal, often disapproving: 'raking in millions', 'rake it in'. Compare 'to coin it' (British), 'to clean up' (make a big profit).

example.target: The app has been raking in cash since launch.
example.en: The app has been earning a great deal of money.

en: money paid regularly to someone, e.g. for the use of their work
literal: originally rights granted by the crown
note: Usually plural: authors and musicians earn royalties; also oil and mining royalties paid to landowners. Compare 'dividends' (shareholders), 'fees', 'commission'.

en: to become worth less over time
literal: Latin pretium, price: to lower the price
note: Cars and currencies depreciate; accountants 'depreciate assets'. Noun 'depreciation'. Opposite 'appreciate'. Not 'deprecate' (disapprove).

example.target: A new car depreciates the moment you drive it away.
example.en: A new car loses value immediately.

en: the money a business has available for daily operations
note: Two words (sometimes 'cashflow' in UK). 'Cash-flow problems' = short of ready money even if profitable. Compare 'liquidity', 'working capital'.

en: a business expense that cannot be recovered; money already spent
literal: cost that has sunk and cannot be raised
note: Economics; 'the sunk cost fallacy' = continuing because of past investment. Also 'to throw good money after bad'.

example.target: The licence fee is a sunk cost; ignore it when deciding.
example.en: The fee is already spent, so it should not affect the decision.

en: to pay out money, especially from a fund or budget
literal: Old French desbourser, to take out of a purse
note: Formal, official: 'funds were disbursed to the regions'. Noun 'disbursement'. Do not confuse with 'disperse' (scatter).

en: a person or company that buys goods to sell at a profit
literal: a man in the middle of the chain
note: 'Cut out the middleman' = buy direct. Plural 'middlemen'; gender-neutral 'intermediary' in formal writing. Compare 'wholesaler', 'broker', 'dealer'.

example.target: Selling online lets farmers cut out the middleman.
example.en: Online selling lets farmers sell directly to customers.

en: a large sum of money given as compensation when someone leaves
note: British 1960s coinage. Related: 'golden parachute' (contractual payout on takeover), 'golden hello' (joining bonus), 'golden handcuffs' (incentives to stay).

en: to reduce the value of a currency officially
note: Economics: 'the pound was devalued in 1967'. Noun 'devaluation'. Figuratively: 'the award has been devalued by over-use'. Compare 'depreciate' (market-driven).

en: a situation where a company cannot pay its debts and closes
note: 'To go into liquidation' (UK); US 'to file for Chapter 7'. A 'liquidator' sells the assets. 'Receivership' and 'administration' are related UK stages.

example.target: The chain went into liquidation last spring.
example.en: The chain of shops closed down and its assets were sold.

en: to invest money in a range of different things to reduce risk
note: 'Diversify a portfolio / into new markets'. Noun 'diversification'. Proverb: 'don't put all your eggs in one basket'.

en: a sudden big fall in the price of shares or a market
literal: probably imitative of falling into mud
note: Noun and verb: 'sales slumped'. Milder than 'crash'; compare 'downturn', 'recession' (technical: two quarters of negative growth), 'depression'.

example.target: A slump in demand forced the factory to cut shifts.
example.en: Falling demand forced the factory to reduce work.

en: money obtained dishonestly through a position of trust
literal: Anglo-French embeseiller, to make away with
note: Legal: 'embezzle company funds'. Compare 'fraud' (general), 'misappropriation' (formal), 'to cook the books' (informal), 'to skim' (take small amounts).

en: to guarantee to pay costs or losses, e.g. of a new issue of shares
literal: to write one's name underneath (a policy)
note: Finance and insurance: 'the bank underwrote the share issue'. Noun 'underwriter'. Figuratively: 'the state underwrites the pension'. Irregular: underwrote/underwritten.

en: profit from selling an asset, taxable in many countries
note: 'Capital gains tax' (CGT). Opposite 'capital loss'. Compare 'income', 'dividends', 'yield'. Usually plural in this sense.

example.target: She paid capital gains on the sale of the flat.
example.en: She paid tax on the profit from selling the flat.

en: to spend money carelessly on unnecessary things
note: Disapproving: 'squander a fortune / an opportunity / a lead'. Compare 'fritter away' (in small amounts), 'splurge' (informal, one big spend), 'blow' (slang).

example.target: He squandered his inheritance in three years.
example.en: He wasted all the money he inherited.

en: a legal claim on property until a debt is paid
note: Legal and finance: 'the bank has a lien on the car'. Pronounced LEEN. Compare 'mortgage', 'collateral' (security offered), 'charge' (UK).

en: a company's total sales over a period
note: British; American 'revenue' or 'sales'. 'Staff turnover' = rate at which employees leave. Not the same as 'profit'.

example.target: Turnover rose, but profits fell.
example.en: Sales increased but profit decreased.

en: the purchase of a company using borrowed money secured on its assets
note: Finance jargon, abbreviated LBO. 'Leverage' (US) = 'gearing' (UK) = ratio of debt to equity. Also a verb: 'to leverage' is business-speak for 'use'.

en: with very little money; hard up
note: Informal; also 'cash-strapped' (journalism: 'cash-strapped councils'). Compare 'skint' (British slang), 'broke', 'hard up'.

example.target: We're a bit strapped for cash until payday.
example.en: We have little money until we get paid.

en: to find money or resources for a project
literal: to attract people by beating a drum
note: Separable: 'drum up support / business / interest'. Informal to neutral. Compare 'to rustle up' (produce quickly), 'to scrape together'.

example.target: They're trying to drum up investment for the new wing.
example.en: They are trying to attract investors for the new wing.

en: a sum of money paid as a bribe to gain an advantage
literal: a payment made with the back of the hand (secretly)
note: British informal; US 'kickback' (usually a share of a contract). Compare 'sweetener' (euphemism), 'bung' (British slang), 'graft' (US).

en: the right to vote in political elections
note: 'Universal suffrage', 'women's suffrage'; 'suffragette' (militant, British) vs 'suffragist'. Formal; everyday word is 'the vote' or 'the franchise'.

en: a small group holding power, often for its own benefit
literal: Greek oligoi, few + archein, to rule
note: 'An oligarch' now usually means a post-Soviet billionaire. Compare 'plutocracy' (rule by the rich), 'autocracy', 'kleptocracy' (rule by thieves).

example.target: Critics say the country has slid into oligarchy.
example.en: Critics say a small wealthy group now controls the country.

en: to officially cancel a law or agreement
literal: Old French rapeler, to call back
note: Laws are repealed; verdicts are 'overturned' or 'quashed'; contracts are 'rescinded'; decisions are 'reversed'. Noun also 'repeal'.

example.target: Parliament voted to repeal the Act.
example.en: Parliament voted to cancel the law.

en: a person's previous criminal conviction, or the record of it
note: American legal slang: 'he has two priors'. British equivalent 'previous' (noun!): 'he's got previous', or formally 'a previous conviction'.

en: the practice of delaying a vote by making long speeches
note: Mainly US Senate; also a verb: 'to filibuster a bill'. In the UK, 'talking out a bill'. Journalistic and political register.

example.target: The bill died after a 14-hour filibuster.
example.en: The bill failed because of a 14-hour delaying speech.

en: to appoint someone to a position by one's own authority
note: Two senses: add a member to a committee without election; and (disapproving) absorb an opponent or idea so it loses its force: 'the movement was co-opted by big brands'.

en: a legal rule or guidance derived from earlier similar cases
note: 'To set a precedent' (law and general use), 'unprecedented' = never seen before. Stress on the first syllable; the adjective 'preceding' is different.

example.target: The ruling sets a worrying precedent for free speech.
example.en: The decision creates a worrying example for future cases.

en: to send someone back to prison or custody until trial
note: British legal: 'remanded in custody' or 'remanded on bail'. US: 'remand' means sending a case back to a lower court. Noun 'on remand'.

en: a person appointed to investigate complaints against organisations
note: Swedish loan (1809 office; adopted in Britain in 1967). Plural 'ombudsmen'; gender-neutral forms 'ombudsperson', 'ombud' exist. 'The Financial Ombudsman'.

example.target: If the bank won't help, complain to the ombudsman.
example.en: If the bank refuses, take it to the independent complaints body.

en: to officially forbid or prohibit something
literal: Latin proscribere, to publish in writing (as outlawed)
note: Formal: 'a proscribed organisation'. Almost the opposite of 'prescribe' (order or recommend), a classic confusable pair.

en: dividing election districts unfairly to favour one party
literal: Governor Elbridge Gerry + salamander (the shape of his 1812 district)
note: American origin, now used worldwide. Verb 'to gerrymander'. Pronounced with a hard or soft g, both heard. Disapproving.

example.target: The map was redrawn in a blatant piece of gerrymandering.
example.en: The boundaries were redrawn unfairly to help one party.

en: disrespect for a court's authority; also deep scorn
note: Legal: 'contempt of court' (can lead to prison); 'to hold someone in contempt'. General: 'beneath contempt'. Adjective 'contemptuous' (scornful) vs 'contemptible' (deserving scorn).

en: a government formed by two or more parties sharing power
note: 'A coalition government'; also 'a coalition of the willing' (military). Compare 'alliance', 'bloc', 'confidence-and-supply agreement' (UK, looser).

en: to make something legal that was previously illegal
literal: to remove from the category of crime
note: British spelling; US 'decriminalize'. Not the same as 'legalise': decriminalised acts may still be regulated or fined. Noun 'decriminalisation'.

example.target: Portugal decriminalised drug possession in 2001.
example.en: Portugal stopped treating drug possession as a crime in 2001.

en: a person who informs on illegal activity inside an organisation
literal: someone blowing a whistle to raise the alarm
note: Neutral to approving; 'to blow the whistle on someone'. One word or hyphenated. Compare 'informer' (negative), 'leaker', 'grass' (British slang).

en: the authority of a court or government to make legal decisions
literal: Latin jus, law + dicere, to say
note: 'Outside our jurisdiction'; also = a territory with its own laws ('tax-friendly jurisdictions'). Formal.

example.target: The court ruled it had no jurisdiction over the dispute.
example.en: The court decided it had no authority to hear the case.

en: an official pardon for people convicted of political offences
note: 'To declare/grant an amnesty'; also 'a tax amnesty', 'a weapons amnesty' (hand in without punishment). Amnesty International, founded 1961.

en: a person who holds extreme political views and seeks radical change
note: Journalistic; may be admiring or hostile: 'a left-wing firebrand'. Compare 'agitator' (negative), 'radical', 'rabble-rouser' (negative).

example.target: The union firebrand called for an all-out strike.
example.en: The militant union leader demanded a full strike.

en: the group of advisers who help a leader; a close circle
note: Neutral: 'the prime minister's inner circle'. Related: 'kitchen cabinet' (unofficial advisers), 'entourage', 'the top brass' (military/informal).

en: to remove a leader from office by force or suddenly
note: Headline word: 'PM ousted in party coup'. Formal-journalistic. Compare 'depose' (monarch), 'topple' (government), 'unseat' (MP), 'impeach' (charge).

example.target: The board ousted the founder after the scandal.
example.en: The board forced the founder out.

en: a careful official study of a public issue or event
note: British spelling for a formal investigation ('a public inquiry'); 'enquiry' for a simple question. American uses 'inquiry' for both. 'To hold / launch an inquiry'.

en: lying under oath in court
literal: Latin per + jurare, to swear falsely
note: Legal: 'to commit perjury', 'to perjure oneself'. Serious crime in common-law countries. Compare 'contempt of court', 'perverting the course of justice' (UK).

example.target: The witness was later charged with perjury.
example.en: The witness was accused of lying under oath.

en: making an exception for one group that others find unfair
note: Usually singular with 'a': 'that's a double standard'. Plural 'double standards' also common in British English. Compare 'hypocrisy', 'one rule for them and another for us'.

en: the policy of a country to stay out of other countries' affairs
note: Twentieth-century American politics; adjective 'isolationist'. Compare 'non-alignment', 'neutrality', 'protectionism' (trade), 'interventionism'.

en: to give official approval or formal consent to something
literal: Latin ratus, fixed + facere, to make
note: Treaties and constitutions are ratified by parliaments. Noun 'ratification'. Compare 'endorse', 'sanction' (which can also mean punish).

example.target: The treaty still has to be ratified by both parliaments.
example.en: Both parliaments still have to formally approve the treaty.

en: to introduce a new product or system gradually to users
literal: to unroll a carpet or a new aircraft from the hangar
note: Separable; noun 'a rollout' (US) / 'roll-out' (UK): 'the vaccine roll-out'. Business and tech register. Compare 'launch', 'deploy' (software), 'phase in'.

example.target: The update will be rolled out to all users next month.
example.en: All users will receive the update gradually next month.

en: able to be proved false by evidence; testable
note: Karl Popper's criterion for a scientific theory. Noun 'falsifiability'. Do not confuse with 'falsified' (faked).

example.target: A claim that cannot be tested is not falsifiable, so it is not science.
example.en: If no evidence could disprove a claim, it is not scientific.

en: to combine two or more things so they can be used together
note: 'Integrate the new software with/into the system'. Noun 'integration'. Also social: 'integrate immigrants'. Opposite 'segregate'.

en: producing the same result on every repetition of an experiment
note: 'The reproducibility crisis' in psychology and medicine (2010s). Compare 'replicable' (another team repeats it), 'robust', 'consistent'.

example.target: The results were not reproducible in other labs.
example.en: Other laboratories could not get the same results.

en: a very small amount that can be measured or detected
note: 'Trace elements' (nutrition), 'traces of explosive'. Also 'trace amounts', 'a trace of irony'. Verb 'to trace' = track down.

en: a thing that causes a process to start or speed up
note: Chemistry: speeds a reaction without being consumed. Figurative: 'a catalyst for change'. Verb 'to catalyse' (UK) / 'catalyze' (US).

example.target: The scandal was the catalyst for reform.
example.en: The scandal triggered the reforms.

en: to test a new scheme on a small scale before full use
note: 'To pilot a scheme' = run a small trial first; 'a pilot study / episode'. Compare 'to trial' (British verb), 'to beta-test', 'to roll out' (launch widely).

en: the gradual process by which species change over generations
note: Darwin's term (1859); Herbert Spencer coined 'survival of the fittest'. Note 'fittest' = best adapted, not strongest. Compare 'evolution' (the result).

en: to find and remove errors from computer code
note: 'Bug' for a fault predates computers (Edison used it in 1878). 'Debugging' and 'a debugger' (tool). Compare 'to patch' (fix with an update), 'to troubleshoot'.

example.target: I spent all night debugging the login page.
example.en: I spent the night fixing errors in the login code.

en: capable of being done; practically possible
note: 'A feasibility study'. Compare 'viable' (can survive or succeed long term), 'practicable' (formal), 'doable' (informal).

en: happening or done at the same moment
note: Technology: 'synchronous communication' (live video) vs 'asynchronous' (email, messaging). Verb 'to synchronise'; informal 'to sync'. Adverb 'synchronously'.

en: the quantity of data that can be transmitted in a given time
note: Technical, but also office slang for mental capacity: 'I don't have the bandwidth for that this week'. Measured in bits per second.

example.target: Sorry, I just don't have the bandwidth to take that on.
example.en: I do not have the capacity to accept that task.

en: at the most advanced stage of development in a field
literal: the sharp edge of a blade that does the cutting
note: Hyphenated before a noun: 'cutting-edge research'; noun phrase 'at the cutting edge'. Synonyms 'state-of-the-art', 'leading-edge', 'bleeding-edge' (so new it is risky).

example.target: The lab does cutting-edge work on battery chemistry.
example.en: The lab does the most advanced battery research.

en: not able to be seen because it is very small or hidden
note: 'An imperceptible nod / change'. Adverb 'imperceptibly' = so gradually that nobody notices. Opposite 'perceptible', 'noticeable'.

example.target: The temperature rose imperceptibly over the decade.
example.en: The temperature rose so slowly that nobody noticed.

en: a tentative explanation to be tested by further investigation
literal: Greek hypo + thesis, a placing under
note: Plural 'hypotheses' (-seez). 'The null hypothesis' in statistics. Verb 'to hypothesise'. Weaker than 'theory', which is well supported by evidence.

en: a mistake caused by a problem in how a program was written
note: Informal; from 1960s astronauts' slang. 'A technical glitch'. Compare 'bug' (code error), 'fault', 'hiccup' (minor problem), 'outage' (service down).

example.target: A glitch in the booking system double-charged customers.
example.en: A software fault charged customers twice.

en: a thing that is no longer useful because something better exists
note: 'Planned obsolescence' = products designed to fail. Compare 'outdated', 'outmoded', 'antiquated' (very old), 'defunct' (no longer existing).

en: to calculate or estimate something approximately
literal: Latin extra + (inter)polate: beyond the known points
note: Statistics: extend a trend beyond the data. 'Extrapolate from the sample'. Warning: 'you can't extrapolate from one case'. Compare 'interpolate', 'project'.

example.target: It's risky to extrapolate from such a small sample.
example.en: Drawing general conclusions from so few cases is risky.

en: a limited amount of something that is shared out
literal: Latin quota pars, how great a part
note: 'Fishing quotas', 'immigration quotas', 'a sales quota'. Compare 'allocation', 'ration' (in shortage), 'cap' (upper limit).

en: a quantity that can change and affects a result
note: Science and programming; 'independent / dependent variable', 'control for a variable'. Adjective sense: 'variable weather'. Compare 'parameter', 'factor'.

en: to become extremely popular on the internet very quickly
note: 2000s coinage; 'a viral video'. Informal to neutral; now standard in journalism. Compare 'to trend', 'to blow up' (slang).

example.target: Her clip went viral overnight.
example.en: Her video became hugely popular in one night.

en: a gap in a law or rule that lets people avoid its purpose
literal: a narrow slit in a castle wall
note: 'To close / exploit a loophole in the law', 'a tax loophole'. Neutral. Compare 'grey area', 'get-out clause' (contract), 'escape hatch'.

en: a person highly skilled in using computers for a purpose
note: Among programmers = clever coder (positive); in the press = intruder (negative); 'ethical hacker', 'white hat' vs 'black hat'. Verb 'to hack into'.

en: an unwanted secondary effect of a drug, action or policy
note: Medicine: 'unwanted side effects'. Figuratively: 'a side effect of the policy'. Compare 'knock-on effect' (British), 'spin-off' (beneficial by-product), 'adverse reaction'.

example.target: Drowsiness is a common side effect of the tablets.
example.en: The tablets often make people sleepy.

en: a leap forward in knowledge or technology; a sudden advance
note: Military origin (breaking an enemy line). 'A medical breakthrough', 'to make a breakthrough'. Compare 'milestone', 'watershed', 'game-changer' (informal).

en: a story or picture with a hidden moral or political meaning
literal: Greek allos + agoreuein, to speak otherwise
note: Orwell's Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution. Adjective 'allegorical'. Compare 'parable' (short moral tale), 'fable' (animals).

en: a short, memorable, often witty statement of a truth
note: Literary; Hippocrates' Aphorisms. Compare 'maxim' (rule of conduct), 'adage' (traditional), 'epigram' (witty, often in verse), 'saying'.

example.target: Wilde's plays are stuffed with aphorisms.
example.en: Wilde's plays are full of short, clever sayings.

en: a literary work imitating another's style to mock it
literal: Italian pasticcio, a pie of mixed ingredients
note: Not always mocking: can be affectionate imitation or a medley of styles. Compare 'parody' (comic exaggeration), 'spoof' (informal), 'homage'.

en: the use of words to mean the opposite, for humour or emphasis
note: Verbal irony (saying the opposite), dramatic irony (audience knows more than characters), situational irony. Often loosely used for 'coincidence'; purists object.

en: a clue in a story that hints at what will happen later
note: Verb 'to foreshadow'. Literary and film criticism. Chekhov's gun: a gun shown in act one must fire by act three.

example.target: The storm in chapter one foreshadows the family's collapse.
example.en: The early storm hints at the later disaster.

en: a work's first printed version or a film's first public showing
note: Noun and verb: 'the film premieres on Friday'. Pronounced PREM-i-air (UK) or prem-EER (US). 'World premiere'. No accent in English.

en: to criticise a work harshly in a review
literal: perhaps from 'to pan out' (gold mining) or hitting with a pan
note: Journalistic: 'the critics panned the play'. Opposite: 'to rave about'. Compare 'slate' (British), 'savage', 'trash' (informal), 'rubbish' (British informal).

example.target: The sequel was panned by almost every critic.
example.en: Nearly every critic gave the sequel a terrible review.

en: the particular group of people a book, film or product is aimed at
note: Marketing and media; 'the demographic' (informal 'the demo' in US TV). Compare 'readership' (publications), 'viewership', 'fan base'.

en: a sudden moment of insight or realisation
note: Religious feast (6 January) and literary term popularised by James Joyce. Now informal too: 'I had an epiphany in the shower'.

example.target: The ending gives the narrator a quiet epiphany.
example.en: At the end the narrator suddenly understands something.

en: a book's or play's final part where everything is resolved
literal: French dénouement, an untying (of the knot)
note: Pronounced day-NOO-mon. Literary. Compare 'climax' (point of greatest tension, comes before), 'resolution', 'epilogue'.

en: a short piece of writing or film that is a brief, vivid description
note: Pronounced vin-YET. Literary and photographic (soft-edged image). Compare 'sketch', 'cameo' (brief appearance by a famous person), 'snapshot'.

en: the deliberate exaggeration used for effect
literal: Greek hyper + ballein, to throw beyond
note: Four syllables: hy-PER-bo-lee. Adjective 'hyperbolic'. Opposite 'understatement' or 'litotes'. Everyday word 'exaggeration'.

example.target: To call it the greatest film ever made is sheer hyperbole.
example.en: Saying it is the best film ever is a wild exaggeration.

en: the most important or most admired part of a collection
literal: the piece at the centre (of a table)
note: British 'centrepiece', US 'centerpiece'. 'The centrepiece of the exhibition / of the reforms'. Compare 'highlight', 'showpiece', 'pièce de résistance'.

en: a person who writes a book for someone else who is named as author
