note: Verb 'to ghostwrite' or simply 'to ghost' (older sense; 'ghosting' now means cutting off contact). Celebrity memoirs are usually ghostwritten.

example.target: Most political memoirs are ghostwritten.
example.en: Most political memoirs are written by someone else.

en: the news media considered as a group, especially newspapers
note: 'The gutter press / tabloid press' (sensational papers), 'press release', 'freedom of the press'. Compare 'the media' (plural noun, often treated as singular).

en: a story that is spread widely but is untrue or exaggerated
note: British 'urban myth', American 'urban legend'. Compare 'hoax' (deliberate deception), 'old wives' tale' (traditional false belief), 'canard' (false report, formal).

en: to shorten a text by removing parts while keeping the sense
note: 'An abridged edition / audiobook'. Noun 'abridgement'. Compare 'condense', 'cut', 'bowdlerise' (remove offensive parts, after Thomas Bowdler).

example.target: The audiobook is abridged, so a few subplots are missing.
example.en: The audiobook is shortened and some side stories are cut.

en: a short clip or extract used to represent a longer work
note: 1980s American TV news; usually disapproving: 'soundbite politics'. Also 'sound bite'. Compare 'quote', 'catchphrase', 'slogan', 'one-liner'.

en: deliberately exaggerated and theatrical in style, often with irony
literal: origin uncertain; possibly French se camper, to pose
note: Adjective and noun: 'high camp', 'a camp performance'. Susan Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' (1964). Compare 'kitsch' (tacky art), 'over the top' (OTT).

en: the typical pattern or main idea that recurs in a work
note: Pronounced mo-TEEF. Music, literature, design: 'a recurring motif'. Compare 'theme' (broader idea), 'leitmotif' (Wagner: musical theme for a character).

example.target: Mirrors are a recurring motif in the novel.
example.en: Mirrors keep appearing as a symbol in the novel.

en: a person who supports artists or causes with money
note: 'Patron of the arts', 'patron saint'; also a regular customer ('patrons are asked...'). Noun 'patronage'. Verb 'to patronise' has the negative sense of talking down.

en: writing or art that is sentimental and of poor quality
note: Informal, American origin. Adjective 'schmaltzy'. Compare 'kitsch', 'mawkish' (formal: sickly sentimental), 'cheesy', 'corny'.

en: a sudden, often unintentional drop from the serious to the trivial
note: Coined by Pope (1727) as the opposite of 'pathos' (feeling). Adjective 'bathetic'. Example: 'He lost his wife, his home and his umbrella.' Literary-critical register.

en: strong public praise from reviewers and critics for a work
note: Fixed collocation, usually 'to win / receive critical acclaim', 'critically acclaimed'. Compare 'plaudits' (formal praise), 'rave reviews', 'a cult following'.

example.target: Her debut novel won widespread critical acclaim.
example.en: Critics praised her first novel highly.

en: a collection of written works by various authors
literal: Greek anthos + legein, a gathering of flowers
note: Poetry, short stories, essays. Compare 'compendium' (reference collection), 'omnibus' (one author's works in one volume), 'compilation' (music).

en: unwilling to reveal one's thoughts or feelings readily
note: Compare 'reserved' (habitually), 'taciturn' (by temperament), 'tight-lipped' (refusing to tell). Often misused to mean 'reluctant'; keep it for silence.

example.target: He was reticent about his years abroad.
example.en: He said little about his time abroad.

en: careful in choosing words so as not to offend; politely cautious
note: Compare 'tactful' (sensitive to feelings), 'discreet' (keeps secrets), 'politic' (prudent, formal), 'circumspect' (cautious in action). 'A diplomatic illness' = a faked excuse.

en: to hint at something without saying it directly
literal: Latin sinus, curve: to wind one's way in
note: Always negative: 'are you insinuating I lied?'. Compare 'imply' (neutral), 'intimate' (formal, gentle), 'suggest'. 'Insinuate oneself into' = worm one's way in.

example.target: The article insinuated that the mayor had taken bribes.
example.en: The article hinted the mayor was corrupt without saying so.

en: expensive and elegant in a showy way; sumptuous
note: Of spending, praise, parties. Compare 'extravagant' (wasteful), 'opulent' (rich and grand), 'luxurious' (comfortable), 'ostentatious' (showing off). Verb: 'lavish praise on'.

en: to look at something quickly and carelessly
literal: to take the top layer off milk
note: Reading verbs: 'skim' (fast, for gist), 'scan' (look for specific details), 'peruse' (formal, careful, though often misused for quick), 'pore over' (study closely).

example.target: I only skimmed the report, so don't quiz me on it.
example.en: I read the report very quickly.

en: not real or genuine; false but claimed as true
note: 'A spurious claim / correlation'. Compare 'specious' (plausible but wrong), 'bogus' (informal, fake), 'counterfeit' (money, goods), 'fallacious' (of reasoning).

en: to walk slowly and with heavy steps, as if tired
note: Walking verbs: 'trudge' (tired, heavy), 'plod' (slow, steady), 'stroll' (leisurely), 'saunter' (casual, confident), 'amble' (relaxed), 'stride' (long purposeful steps).

example.target: We trudged home through the snow.
example.en: We walked home wearily through the snow.

en: to look at someone angrily or threateningly
note: Looking verbs: 'glare' (angry stare), 'glower' (sullen, brooding), 'scowl' (frown angrily), 'gaze' (long, steady), 'peer' (look closely, with difficulty), 'ogle' (stare lustfully).

en: experienced in life and not easily shocked by human weakness
note: Compare 'sophisticated' (cultured), 'urbane' (smooth, courteous), 'cosmopolitan' (international), 'street-smart' (US) / 'streetwise' (UK). 'Worldly goods' = possessions.

en: deserving blame or criticism for a fault
note: Legal flavour: 'culpable homicide' (Scotland). Compare 'guilty' (legally), 'to blame', 'at fault', 'responsible', 'liable' (legally answerable for cost).

en: to laugh quietly or in a suppressed way, often at something private
note: Laughing verbs: 'chuckle' (quiet, amused), 'giggle' (silly, nervous), 'snigger' UK / 'snicker' US (unkind), 'guffaw' (loud), 'titter' (nervous, suppressed), 'cackle' (harsh).

example.target: He chuckled to himself over the cartoon.
example.en: He laughed quietly at the cartoon.

en: very old-fashioned and no longer suitable or used
note: Disapproving: 'antiquated machinery / attitudes'. Compare 'antique' (old and valuable), 'archaic' (of language), 'obsolete' (replaced), 'dated' (slightly old-fashioned), 'vintage' (admired).

en: to look at something fixed and open-mouthed in surprise
literal: Old Norse gapa, to open the mouth
note: 'Gape at'. Compare 'gawp' (British, stupidly), 'gawk' (US), 'stare' (neutral), 'gaze' (admiring). Adjective 'gaping' = wide open ('a gaping hole').

en: confident and stylish in a slightly daring way
note: 'A jaunty hat / tune / walk'. Compare 'perky' (cheerful), 'dapper' (neatly dressed man), 'debonair' (charming, suave), 'rakish' (dashingly careless).

example.target: He wore his cap at a jaunty angle.
example.en: He wore his cap tilted in a cheerful, confident way.

en: to repair or improve something old; restore
note: Buildings and devices: 'a refurbished phone'. Compare 'renovate' (building, major work), 'restore' (to original state), 'revamp' (informal, new look), 'do up' (British informal).

en: to cry noisily and with heavy breathing
note: Crying verbs: 'sob' (loud, gasping), 'weep' (literary, quiet), 'whimper' (soft, frightened), 'wail' (loud, drawn-out), 'blubber' (informal, childishly), 'snivel' (sniffing, pathetic).

example.target: She sobbed through the whole final scene.
example.en: She cried loudly during the last scene.

en: lasting for a very short time
note: Literary: 'ephemeral fame'. Compare 'fleeting' (passing quickly), 'transient' (passing through), 'transitory' (formal), 'short-lived', 'momentary'. Noun 'ephemera' = disposable printed items.

en: to speak in a low, indistinct voice
note: Speaking verbs: 'mumble' (indistinct), 'mutter' (low, often complaining), 'murmur' (soft, pleasant), 'whisper' (no voice), 'grumble' (complain), 'drone' (monotonous).

en: to shine with a soft, flickering light
note: Light verbs: 'shimmer' (wavering), 'glimmer' (faint), 'glisten' (wet surface), 'gleam' (reflected), 'glint' (brief flash), 'glow' (steady warm), 'twinkle' (stars, eyes), 'sparkle' (many flashes).

example.target: The lake shimmered in the evening sun.
example.en: The lake shone with a soft, moving light.

en: to refuse to accept something; reject firmly
note: Literary, strong: 'spurned his advances', 'a spurned lover'. Compare 'rebuff' (snub), 'decline' (politely), 'turn down' (neutral), 'reject', 'shun' (avoid a person).

en: a smell, especially a pleasant one
note: Smell words: 'scent' (pleasant, animal trail), 'aroma' (food, coffee), 'fragrance' (perfume, flowers), 'odour' (neutral-to-bad), 'stench'/'stink' (very bad), 'whiff' (brief), 'pong' (British informal).

en: to break suddenly and violently into many small pieces
note: Breaking verbs: 'shatter' (glass, into fragments), 'smash' (violently), 'crack' (line without separating), 'snap' (clean break of something thin), 'crumble' (to powder), 'splinter' (wood).

example.target: The vase shattered on the tiles.
example.en: The vase broke into many pieces on the floor.

en: too confident, in a way that annoys people
note: Informal. Scale: 'self-assured' (positive), 'assertive' (positive), 'cocky' (irritating), 'arrogant' (contemptuous of others), 'conceited' (vain), 'smug' (pleased with oneself).

en: to steal something small of little value
note: Stealing verbs: 'pilfer' (small items, often from work), 'filch'/'nick'/'pinch' (informal), 'swipe' (US informal), 'shoplift', 'embezzle' (funds), 'loot' (in riots), 'plunder' (war).

example.target: Someone has been pilfering pens from the stationery cupboard.
example.en: Someone keeps stealing pens from the supply cupboard.

en: to walk in a proud, confident way to attract attention
literal: Old English strutian, to stand out stiffly
note: Compare 'swagger' (arrogant, rolling walk), 'prance' (springy, showy), 'parade', 'sashay' (US, gliding). 'Strut your stuff' = show off (informal).

en: to achieve a balance between two competing demands
literal: to hit the point of balance on a scale
note: 'Strike a balance between X and Y'. Also 'strike a deal / a chord / a note / a pose'. Irregular: strike/struck.

example.target: We need to strike a balance between speed and accuracy.
example.en: We must balance speed against accuracy.

en: a very large amount of money or a very high price
note: 'Hefty' collocates with sum, fine, price tag, bill, increase. Also 'a tidy sum' (ironically modest), 'a princely sum' (ironic), 'a small fortune'.

en: to have a strong, lasting effect on someone or something
note: Impression collocates: make/leave/create an impression; a lasting, favourable, false, fleeting impression; 'be under the impression that'.

example.target: Her speech left a lasting impression on the students.
example.en: The students remembered her speech for a long time.

en: heavy rain falling continuously
note: Natives say 'torrential rain', 'driving rain', 'pouring rain', never 'strong rain'. Also 'it's bucketing down' (British), 'a downpour', 'a cloudburst'.

en: to make a decision after much thought
note: Decision verbs: make, reach, come to, arrive at; 'a snap decision' (fast), 'a unanimous decision', 'the final decision rests with'. Not 'take a decision' in US English (acceptable in UK).

en: complete and utter failure or chaos
literal: a disaster with nothing to soften it
note: 'Unmitigated' pairs almost only with negatives: disaster, failure, nonsense, gall. Other intensifiers: 'an abject failure', 'a resounding success', 'a sheer waste'.

example.target: The launch party was an unmitigated disaster.
example.en: The launch party was a total failure.

en: to think about an idea seriously and carefully
note: Formal; 'give careful / due / further consideration to'. 'Take into consideration' = take into account. Conversational: 'give it some thought'.

en: a very strong, deep-rooted belief
note: Belief collocates: deeply/firmly/widely held, strong, unshakeable, misguided; 'beyond belief' = incredible; 'contrary to popular belief'.

en: to not succeed in reaching a standard or expectation
literal: to land short of the target
note: 'Fall short of expectations / the target / the mark'. 'Fall woefully short' (strong). Irregular: fall/fell/fallen. Compare 'live up to' (meet).

example.target: Sales fell well short of the forecast.
example.en: Sales were much lower than predicted.

en: complete silence, with nobody speaking or moving
literal: a silence so loud it deafens (oxymoron)
note: Used of a pointed refusal to respond: 'the proposal was met with a deafening silence'. Also 'stony silence', 'an awkward silence', 'to break the silence'.

en: to pay close attention to detail
note: Attention collocates: pay/draw/attract/divert attention; close, undivided, scant attention; 'attention to detail' is a CV cliché. Irregular: pay/paid.

en: to start a difficult task with energy and purpose
literal: to set a ball in motion
note: Informal to neutral: 'to get/start/set the ball rolling'. Also 'keep the ball rolling' (maintain momentum), 'the ball is in your court'.

example.target: Let's get the ball rolling with a quick round of introductions.
example.en: Let's start with brief introductions.

en: a feeling of dread that something bad is about to happen
note: 'I had a sinking feeling that...' = I dreaded. Related: 'my heart sank', 'a gut feeling' (instinct), 'a nagging feeling' (persistent doubt).

en: to make small changes to improve something
note: 'Fine-tune the details / the engine / the proposal'. Compare 'tweak' (informal, small adjustment), 'hone' (perfect a skill), 'polish' (final improvements).

example.target: We're still fine-tuning the schedule.
example.en: We are still making small adjustments to the timetable.

en: in a state of complete hopelessness and misery
literal: at the bottom of a deep place
note: Fixed phrase; 'to plumb the depths' = reach the lowest point. Other despair collocates: 'drive someone to despair', 'in sheer despair', 'a counsel of despair'.

en: to express strong disagreement or objection
note: 'Voice' as verb pairs with concerns, doubts, objections, opinions, support. Also 'raise concerns', 'allay concerns' (calm them), 'address concerns'.

example.target: Several residents voiced concerns about the traffic.
example.en: Several residents said they were worried about traffic.

en: with no possibility of change or improvement
note: 'Damaged beyond repair / recognition / belief / doubt'. 'Beyond' as a limit marker: 'beyond redemption', 'beyond the pale' (unacceptable), 'beyond reproach'.

en: to receive many angry complaints or criticism
note: British-flavoured: 'come in for heavy / fierce / sharp criticism'. Also 'draw criticism', 'face a backlash', 'be on the receiving end of'. Irregular: come/came.

example.target: The referee came in for fierce criticism after the match.
example.en: The referee was strongly criticised after the match.

en: a great amount of effort put into something
note: Strictly means joint effort by several people, now often just 'determined'. Effort collocates: make/spare no/redouble one's effort; a valiant, half-hearted, last-ditch effort.

en: to accept responsibility and deal with a problem
literal: to become the owner of a problem
note: Management-speak since the 1990s: 'take ownership of your mistakes'. Older: 'take responsibility for', 'own up to' (admit), 'shoulder the blame'.

en: the busiest or most intense part of an activity
literal: the thickest part of a battle
note: 'In the thick of it / of the action / of things' = at the busiest, most intense point. British sitcom title (2005). Compare 'in the thick of battle', 'at the sharp end'.

example.target: By nine o'clock the kitchen was in the thick of it.
example.en: By nine the kitchen was at its busiest.

en: to state one's position clearly and refuse to change it
literal: to stand firmly in one place
note: 'Take a stand on/against', 'make a stand'. Compare 'put one's foot down' (informal, refuse), 'dig one's heels in' (stubbornly), 'hold the line'.

en: to feel extremely satisfied; be very pleased with success
literal: jumping over the moon, as the cow in the nursery rhyme
note: British informal, famously a footballers' cliché ('over the moon' vs 'sick as a parrot'). Americans say 'thrilled to bits' or 'on cloud nine'.

example.target: She was over the moon about the job offer.
example.en: She was delighted about the job offer.

en: to make a strong argument with great passion
note: Argue + adverb: passionately, persuasively, convincingly, forcefully, cogently, vehemently (angrily). 'Argue the toss' (British) = dispute a decision pointlessly.

en: a crime or wrong that is very serious and obvious
note: 'Flagrant' collocates with breach, violation, disregard, abuse. Compare 'blatant' (shameless, obvious), 'gross' (misconduct, negligence), 'egregious' (shockingly bad).

example.target: Sharing the data was a flagrant breach of the agreement.
example.en: Sharing the data obviously and seriously broke the agreement.

en: loving or attracted to; a lover of something
note: Examples: bibliophile (books), Anglophile, audiophile, philanthropy (love of humankind), philosophy (love of wisdom), philharmonic. Opposite: -phobe, -phobia (fear).

example.target: A true bibliophile never has enough shelves.
example.en: A book-lover always needs more shelves.

en: fear or hatred of something
note: Examples: claustrophobia (enclosed spaces), arachnophobia (spiders), xenophobia (foreigners), technophobe, hydrophobia (old name for rabies). Adjective -phobic.

en: good, well, pleasant
note: Examples: euphemism (pleasant way of speaking), euphoria (feeling well), eulogy (good words at a funeral), eugenics, euthanasia (good death), evangelist (good news).

en: bad, difficult, abnormal
note: Examples: dystopia (bad place; opposite of utopia), dyslexia (difficulty with words), dysfunctional, dyspepsia (indigestion), dystrophy. Not the same as 'dis-' (apart, not).

example.target: The novel paints a chilling dystopia.
example.en: The novel describes a frightening imaginary bad society.

en: around, surrounding
note: Examples: circumnavigate (sail around), circumvent (go around an obstacle or rule), circumspect (looking around, cautious), circumstance, circumlocution (talking around a point).

en: writing, drawing, recording
note: Examples: autograph (self-writing), calligraphy (beautiful writing), choreography, seismograph, biography, orthography (correct writing, spelling), hagiography (saint's life; now flattering biography).

en: to carry, to bear
note: Examples: transfer (carry across), refer (carry back), confer (bring together), defer (carry away, postpone), infer, vociferous (carrying the voice), conifer (cone-bearing), fertile.

en: to lead, to bring
note: Examples: induce, deduce (lead down from), seduce (lead astray), produce, conduct, abduct (lead away), aqueduct (water-leader), ductile (can be drawn out), duke (leader).

example.target: From the footprints we can deduce he left in a hurry.
example.en: The footprints let us reason that he left quickly.

en: other, different (hetero-) versus same (homo-)
note: Pairs: heterogeneous/homogeneous (mixed/uniform), heterodox/orthodox, homonym (same name), homophone (same sound). 'Homo' in Homo sapiens is Latin for man, a different root.

en: time
note: Examples: chronic (long-lasting; not 'severe'), chronology, anachronism (out of its time), synchronise, chronicle. Pronounced with a hard k.

example.target: A wristwatch in a Roman epic is a glaring anachronism.
example.en: A watch in a Roman film is an obvious error of time period.

en: word, speech, reason, study
note: Examples: etymology (true meaning of words), tautology (same word twice), neologism (new word), eulogy, dialogue, monologue, epilogue, analogy, logistics (from a different root!).

en: to speak, to say
note: Examples: dictate, contradict (speak against), verdict (true saying), predict, edict (official saying), jurisdiction, benediction (good saying), indict (accuse; silent c: in-DITE).

en: to see, to look
note: Examples: inspect, retrospect (looking back), prospect (looking forward), circumspect, conspicuous (easily seen), perspicacious (seeing through, shrewd), auspicious (favourable bird-watching omen).

example.target: In retrospect, selling the house was a mistake.
example.en: Looking back, selling the house was wrong.

en: to hold, to keep
note: Examples: retain, detain (hold away), abstain (hold back from), sustain (hold up), tenacious (holding fast), tenet (a held belief), tenure, untenable (cannot be held, of an argument).

en: self, by oneself
note: Examples: autonomy (self-rule), autocrat, autodidact (self-taught person), autobiography, automaton, autopsy (seeing for oneself). 'Automobile' mixes Greek and Latin, a classic hybrid.

en: people, the common people
note: Examples: democracy, demagogue (leader of the people, now rabble-rouser), demographics, endemic (within a people, of disease), pandemic (all the people), epidemic (upon the people).

example.target: The press branded him a demagogue.
example.en: The newspapers called him a politician who stirs up the crowd.

en: to break
note: Examples: interrupt (break between), disrupt, erupt (break out), abrupt (broken off), corrupt (broken thoroughly), rupture, bankrupt (from Italian banca rotta, broken bench).

en: death
note: Examples: mortal, immortal, mortuary, mortgage (dead pledge), moribund (dying), post-mortem, mortify (originally 'kill the flesh'; now 'embarrass deeply'), memento mori.

example.target: The high street's bookshops are moribund.
example.en: The town's bookshops are close to dying out.

en: beside, beyond, contrary to
note: Examples: paradox (beside opinion), parasite (eating beside), paragraph, parallel, paramedic (beside the doctor), paranormal. Different root in 'parachute, parasol' (Italian parare, to shield).

en: to put, to place
note: Examples: impose, juxtapose (place side by side), expose, depose (put down, remove a ruler), postpone (put after), component, proponent (one who puts forward), exponent.

en: under, below
note: Latin sub-: subterranean, subliminal (below the threshold), subjugate (put under the yoke), subpoena (under penalty). Greek hypo-: hypothermia, hypodermic (under the skin), hypocrisy.

en: above, over, beyond
note: Latin: supersede (sit above; note the spelling, not -cede), superfluous (overflowing), supercilious (raised eyebrow). Greek: hyperbole, hyperactive, hypertension. Opposites of sub-/hypo-.

example.target: The waiter's supercilious smile put us off the place.
example.en: The waiter's arrogant smile spoiled the restaurant for us.

en: to send
note: Examples: transmit, omit (send away, leave out), remit (send back; noun = area of responsibility), emissary (one sent out), missive (a letter), intermittent (sending between, stopping and starting).

en: to believe, to trust
note: Examples: credible (believable), credulous (too ready to believe), incredulous (unable to believe), credentials, creed, credit (originally trust), accreditation. Credible vs credulous is a classic trap.

example.target: Only the most credulous readers fell for the hoax.
example.en: Only readers who believe too easily were fooled.

en: many
note: Greek: polyglot (many tongues), polymath (many learnings), polygon, polyphony. Latin: multitude, multifarious (of many kinds), multilateral. Opposites: mono-/uni- (one), oligo-/pauci- (few).

en: in any case; used to return to the main point or dismiss an issue
note: Informal variant of 'anyway'; 'anyhow' as a manner adverb means carelessly ('things were thrown in anyhow'). 'Anyways' is non-standard US. Spoken discourse marker.

example.target: Anyhow, that's enough about me.
example.en: In any case, let's stop talking about me.

en: in a way that is appropriate to what has just been mentioned
note: Two uses: manner ('plan accordingly') and connector ('= therefore', formal). Position: sentence-initial or after the verb. Compare 'consequently', 'hence', 'thus'.

example.target: The forecast is for snow; dress accordingly.
example.en: Snow is forecast, so dress for it.

en: used to say what is true despite what has just been said
note: Formal; one word. 'Nevertheless' is interchangeable; 'notwithstanding' is more formal; 'still' and 'all the same' are conversational. 'None the less' as three words is now dated.

en: used to add a stronger or more surprising point to a previous one
note: Three uses: intensifier ('very good indeed', British), confirmation ('Indeed.'), and escalation ('difficult, indeed impossible'). Can sound pompous if overused.

example.target: The plan is risky; indeed, it may be illegal.
example.en: The plan is risky and, more than that, possibly illegal.

en: used to introduce something that contrasts with what came before
note: Formal; introduces the reverse case, not just a contrast: 'Exercise helps sleep; conversely, poor sleep makes exercise harder'. Often misused for 'on the other hand'.

en: used to say that something is true in a certain sense only
note: Concession marker: 'Admittedly, the data are limited, but...'. Formal to neutral. Compare 'granted', 'to be fair', 'to be sure' (US/literary), 'I grant you'.

example.target: Admittedly, I hadn't read the small print.
example.en: I must admit I had not read the details.

en: as a result; because of something previously mentioned
note: Formal; usually followed by -ing: 'he resigned, thereby avoiding a vote'. Family of 'there-' compounds: thereafter, therein, thereof, thereupon, mostly legal.

en: in an extremely surprising way; it is hard to believe that
note: Sentence adverb expressing the speaker's attitude ('Astonishingly, nobody was hurt') or degree ('astonishingly cheap'). Compare 'remarkably', 'incredibly' (informal), 'staggeringly'.

en: used to introduce an example or make something more specific
note: Introduces the precise identity: 'two languages, namely Welsh and Breton'. Formal; Latin 'viz.' (videlicet) in older texts; 'to wit' in legal English; 'i.e.' in writing.

example.target: One group benefits most, namely first-time buyers.
example.en: The group that benefits most is first-time buyers.

en: said to admit that the other person has a good point
note: British conversational concession, often then followed by 'but'. American: 'fair point', 'OK, fine'. Also 'point taken', 'I'll give you that'.

example.target: Fair enough, but we still need a backup plan.
example.en: I accept that, but we still need a backup.

en: in an unspoken or implied way; without being stated directly
note: 'Tacitly agree / approve / accept'. Adjective 'tacit' ('tacit knowledge' = know-how that is hard to put into words). Compare 'implicitly', 'by default'.

en: used to introduce a summary or conclusion
literal: small enough to fit inside a nut's shell
note: From Pliny's story of the Iliad copied so small it fitted in a nutshell. Informal to neutral. Formal: 'in sum', 'in short', 'to summarise'.

example.target: In a nutshell, we ran out of money.
example.en: To put it briefly, we ran out of money.

en: used to introduce a correction to something just said
note: Self-repair marker: 'I spoke to the manager, or rather, to her deputy'. Compare 'I mean' (informal), 'that is to say' (formal), 'let me rephrase that'.

en: used to introduce a fact that supports the point being made
note: Two meanings: a reminder of a reason ('he's only six, after all') and 'despite expectations' ('it didn't rain after all'). Position changes the meaning: initial = reason, final = contrary to expectation.

example.target: Don't blame her; after all, she wasn't even there.
example.en: Don't blame her, because she was not there.

en: without doubt; used to emphasise certainty
note: Stance adverb: 'undeniably talented'. Set: 'undoubtedly', 'unquestionably', 'indisputably', 'arguably' (= can be argued, weaker), 'admittedly'.

en: used before giving a more precise or correct statement
note: 'A dozen eggs, thirteen to be precise'. Also 'to be exact', 'more precisely', 'strictly speaking' (correct according to rules), 'technically' (informal).

en: despite what one might expect; strangely
note: Sentence adverb: 'Paradoxically, the cuts increased spending'. Compare 'ironically' (loosely 'strangely'), 'curiously', 'oddly enough', 'counter-intuitively'.

example.target: Paradoxically, the safety rules made the road more dangerous.
example.en: Strangely, the rules meant to make the road safer did the opposite.

en: used to signal that one is about to change the subject
literal: let that be as it may be
note: Formal, slightly old-fashioned concession: 'Be that as it may, we have a deadline'. Preserves the old subjunctive 'be'. Compare 'even so', 'that said', 'regardless'.

example.target: Be that as it may, the rules still apply to you.
example.en: Even if that is true, the rules apply to you anyway.

en: used to introduce an additional, often stronger, point
note: Formal written connector; sentence-initial. Family: 'furthermore', 'what is more' (more emphatic), 'in addition', 'besides' (informal), 'on top of that' (spoken).

en: so to speak; used to signal a loose or figurative expression
note: Formal, British-flavoured hedge marking a metaphor: 'he is the firm's conscience, as it were'. Compare 'so to speak', 'in a manner of speaking', 'if you like'.

example.target: She's the glue holding the team together, as it were.
example.en: Figuratively speaking, she keeps the team united.

en: in a careful or qualified way; with reservations
note: 'Tentatively agree', 'a tentative date' (provisional). Hedge adverb family: 'provisionally', 'arguably', 'conceivably', 'ostensibly'.

en: from a different and more important point of view
note: Spoken and written; signals that what follows matters more: 'It's expensive and, more to the point, unnecessary'. Compare 'more importantly', 'what's more'.

en: used to introduce a remark that is relevant only in passing
note: Topic-shift marker: 'Incidentally, did you ever get that refund?'. Informal 'by the way', formal 'parenthetically', dated 'apropos'. Also = by chance.

example.target: Incidentally, I bumped into your brother yesterday.
example.en: By the way, I met your brother yesterday.

en: used to say that something is true to a large extent
literal: nautical: sailing both into and off the wind
note: Seventeenth-century sailing phrase. Neutral: 'By and large, the scheme worked'. Compare 'on the whole', 'generally speaking', 'for the most part', 'all things considered'.

en: in the time before now; previously
note: Adjective (and rarely adverb): 'his erstwhile colleague' = former. Literary, often ironic. Compare 'former', 'one-time', 'sometime' (formal: 'sometime editor of The Times'), 'quondam'.

example.target: She was greeted warmly by her erstwhile rival.
example.en: Her former rival greeted her warmly.

en: the use of mocking remarks meant to hurt or ridicule
note: Sarcasm is a form of irony with intent to wound; irony need not be. Adjective 'sarcastic', informal 'sarky' (British). 'Sarcasm is the lowest form of wit' (attributed to Wilde).

en: treating serious issues with inappropriate humour
note: Pronounced fa-SEE-shus; one of the few English words with a, e, i, o, u in order. Disapproving: 'I was only being facetious' = half-apology for a joke.

example.target: Don't be facetious; this is a funeral.
example.en: Stop making inappropriate jokes at a funeral.

en: dry, understated humour delivered with a straight face
note: American vaudeville 1920s. Adjective, adverb and verb: 'she deadpanned'. Comedians Buster Keaton, Jack Dee. Compare 'dry', 'wry', 'poker-faced'.

example.target: He delivered the line completely deadpan and the room erupted.
example.en: He said it with no expression and everyone laughed.

en: showing a slightly mocking amusement at a bad situation
note: 'A wry smile / comment'. Adverb 'wryly'. Suggests dry, self-aware humour about misfortune. Compare 'rueful' (regretful), 'sardonic' (bitter, scornful).

en: deliberately making something seem less important than it is
note: Classic British humour: 'a bit of a problem' for a catastrophe. 'That's an understatement!' Literary term 'litotes' ('not bad'). Opposite 'hyperbole'.

example.target: To say the trip was eventful is something of an understatement.
example.en: The trip was far more than merely eventful.

en: a joke that plays on two meanings of a word
literal: origin uncertain; perhaps Italian puntiglio, fine point
note: The groan is the traditional reaction; 'no pun intended' acknowledges an accidental one. Formal term 'paronomasia'. Verb 'to pun'. 'Punster' (one who puns).

en: scornfully mocking in a cynical way
literal: Greek sardonios, of Sardinia (a plant there supposedly caused grimacing)
note: 'A sardonic laugh / grin'. Darker and more contemptuous than 'wry' or 'sarcastic'. Literary register.

example.target: He raised a sardonic eyebrow at the minister's promise.
example.en: He showed cynical mockery at the promise.

en: the use of exaggeration or ridicule to expose faults, especially in politics
note: Swift, Private Eye, The Onion. Adjective 'satirical', verb 'to satirise'. Not from 'satyr'. Compare 'lampoon' (personal attack), 'parody', 'send-up' (British).

en: an imitation that mocks a person or style; also a gentle mockery
note: British informal; verb 'to send up'. 'A send-up of the royal family'. American equivalent 'a spoof' or 'a takeoff'. Compare 'parody', 'lampoon'.

example.target: The sketch was a merciless send-up of reality TV.
example.en: The sketch mocked reality television without pity.

en: so funny and ridiculous as to be absurd
literal: from 'farce', French: stuffing (comic interludes stuffed into plays)
note: Of situations rather than jokes: 'a farcical trial'. Noun 'farce' = chaotic comedy or an absurd process. Disapproving when applied to real events.

en: words or expressions used by a particular group that outsiders find hard to understand
literal: Old French jargon, chatter of birds
note: Disapproving: 'management jargon', 'legal jargon'. Compare 'terminology' (neutral), 'slang' (informal, in-group), 'argot' (criminal/secret), 'cant' (hypocritical talk).

en: a mild or indirect word used instead of a blunt one
note: 'Passed away' (died), 'let go' (sacked), 'collateral damage'. Opposite 'dysphemism' (harsh term). Adjective 'euphemistic'; 'euphemistically speaking'.

example.target: 'Downsizing' is just a euphemism for sacking people.
example.en: 'Downsizing' is a softer word for dismissing staff.

en: the informal, often humorous style of spoken everyday language
note: Dictionary label 'colloq.' marks words fine in speech but not formal writing. Noun 'a colloquialism'. Not the same as 'slang' (more restricted) or 'vulgar'.

en: excessively formal and self-important in speech or manner
note: 'Pompous prose / official'. Noun 'pomposity'. Compare 'bombastic' (inflated language), 'grandiloquent', 'highfalutin' (informal, US), 'stuffy'.

example.target: The letter was so pompous we read it aloud for laughs.
example.en: The letter was so self-important we found it funny.

en: an expression of mild humour that gently makes fun
literal: pushing the tongue into the cheek to suppress a smile
note: Adjective or adverb: 'a tongue-in-cheek remark', 'said tongue in cheek'. Hyphenate before a noun. Neutral; signals the speaker is not serious.

en: using more words than are needed; wordy
note: Disapproving: 'a verbose report'. Noun 'verbosity'. Compare 'wordy', 'long-winded', 'prolix' (formal), 'rambling', 'garrulous' (of people).

en: a quick, clever and amusing remark
note: Noun and verb: 'he quipped that...'. A quick witty remark. Compare 'wisecrack' (US, flippant), 'one-liner', 'witticism', 'bon mot' (French, elegant).

example.target: She defused the row with a well-timed quip.
example.en: She ended the argument with a quick joke.

en: using language that is coarse, rude or crude
note: 'Ribald jokes / songs' = sexual, vulgar but good-humoured. Pronounced RIB-ald. Compare 'bawdy' (cheerfully indecent), 'lewd' (offensive), 'risqué' (daring), 'blue' (British: 'a blue joke').

en: stiff, old-fashioned and overly concerned with correctness
note: Often 'prim and proper'. Disapproving, usually of women in older usage; now of attitudes. Compare 'prudish' (shocked by sex), 'strait-laced', 'priggish' (self-righteous).

en: old-fashioned language that is no longer in everyday use
note: Dictionary label 'arch.': thee, thou, hither, methinks, ere. Used deliberately for humour or solemnity. Compare 'obsolete' (no longer used at all), 'dated', 'literary'.

example.target: 'Whence' sounds archaic, but lawyers still write it.
example.en: 'Whence' is old-fashioned, yet lawyers use it.

en: treating a trivial subject in grand epic style for comic effect
note: Literary: Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' treats a stolen curl like an epic battle. Adjective. Everyday equivalent: describing trivia in grand language for comic effect.

en: a short joke or witty remark delivered in a single sentence
note: Stand-up comedy term; also 'a zinger' (US, sharp retort), 'a put-down' (insult), 'a gag' (British, any joke), 'a punchline' (the funny end of a joke).

en: a statement that is so obvious or dull it is laughable
note: Disapproving: 'empty platitudes', 'to mouth platitudes'. Adjective 'platitudinous'. Compare 'cliché', 'truism', 'banality', 'bromide' (US, soothing commonplace).

example.target: The speech was nothing but platitudes about teamwork.
example.en: The speech was only dull, obvious remarks about teamwork.

en: so refined and elegant as to seem affected
note: Now usually ironic: 'genteel poverty', 'a genteel seaside town'. Noun 'gentility'. Compare 'refined' (positive), 'twee' (British, affectedly quaint), 'dainty'.

en: to speak bluntly and plainly about something
target: to call a spade a spade
literal: to name the gardening tool by its plain name
note: Erasmus mistranslated Plutarch's 'trough' as 'spade'. 'Plain-spoken', 'forthright', 'blunt', 'no-nonsense'. Not racial in origin, but some avoid it in the US because of a later slur.

example.target: She calls a spade a spade, which some colleagues find bracing.
example.en: She speaks bluntly, which some find refreshing or harsh.

en: a person who enjoys and knows a lot about good food
note: Also adjective: 'gourmet food'. Compare 'gourmand' (eats a lot), 'foodie' (informal), 'epicure' (refined pleasure), 'connoisseur' (expert judge). Pronounced GOOR-may.

en: pleasantly sharp or bitter in taste; also sharply critical
note: 'Tart apples', 'a tart reply'. Taste words: 'tangy' (pleasantly sharp), 'sour', 'acidic', 'astringent' (makes the mouth pucker), 'bitter'. Also a pastry.

example.target: The rhubarb was deliciously tart.
example.en: The rhubarb was pleasantly sour.

en: having a pleasantly rich, deep, non-sweet flavour
note: British 'savoury', US 'savory'. Opposite of 'sweet' in British food talk: 'a savoury snack'. 'Umami' is the technical fifth taste. 'Unsavoury' = morally unpleasant.

en: to eat or drink greedily in large amounts
note: 'Gorge (oneself) on chocolate'. Compare 'binge' (uncontrolled), 'overindulge' (formal, polite), 'pig out' (slang), 'stuff one's face' (informal).

example.target: We gorged ourselves on oysters by the harbour.
example.en: We ate huge amounts of oysters by the harbour.

en: a hidden, little-known place that is very good
note: Travel-writing cliché: 'the restaurant is a hidden gem'. Related: 'off the beaten track' (remote), 'a well-kept secret', 'a find', 'undiscovered'.

en: to wander slowly with no particular aim; to wind
literal: the winding river Maeander in Turkey
note: Of rivers, roads, people and speeches ('a meandering talk'). Compare 'wander', 'roam', 'ramble' (walk for pleasure; also talk aimlessly), 'drift'.

example.target: We meandered through the old town with no map.
example.en: We wandered slowly through the old town.

en: tiredness and confusion after a long flight across time zones
note: 1960s coinage; two words, adjective 'jet-lagged'. 'To get over jet lag'. Related: 'red-eye' (overnight flight), 'layover' / 'stopover', 'long-haul'.

en: a journey undertaken for a specific purpose, often difficult
literal: Latin expedire, to free the feet
note: 'A shopping expedition' (jokey), 'a polar expedition'. Compare 'excursion' (short trip), 'jaunt' (short pleasure trip), 'trek' (long hard walk), 'pilgrimage', 'odyssey'.

en: a very quick trip with many brief stops
literal: stopping briefly at small stations when the whistle sounded
note: American rail politics (campaign speeches from the train). Now 'a whistle-stop tour of Europe' = very quick, many stops. Journalistic.

example.target: The minister made a whistle-stop tour of five capitals in three days.
example.en: The minister visited five capitals very briefly in three days.

en: unplanned and done on impulse
literal: driven by a spur at that very moment
note: Adjective before a noun ('a spur-of-the-moment decision'); 'on the spur of the moment' as adverbial. Compare 'impromptu', 'spontaneous', 'off the cuff' (of speech).

en: to enjoy food, drink or an experience slowly and fully
note: British 'savour', US 'savor'. Figurative: 'savour the moment / victory'. Compare 'relish' (enjoy greatly), 'sip' (small mouthfuls), 'nurse a drink' (make it last).

example.target: Savour it slowly; that bottle cost a fortune.
example.en: Drink it slowly and enjoy it; it was expensive.

en: a small amount of food eaten between meals
note: Plural 'nibbles' = party snacks (British). Verb 'to nibble (at/on)'. Compare 'a bite' (quick meal), 'a morsel' (small piece), 'a snack', 'finger food', 'canapés'.

en: unpleasantly strong and bitter in smell or taste
note: Mostly of smoke, smells and fumes: 'acrid smoke'. Figurative: 'an acrid exchange'. Compare 'pungent' (strong-smelling, e.g. cheese), 'rancid' (fat gone off), 'astringent'.

example.target: Acrid smoke from the barbecue drifted across the garden.
example.en: Harsh, bitter smoke drifted across the garden.

en: a person who has travelled widely and is at ease anywhere
literal: one who trots around the globe
note: Informal, slightly dated; verb 'to globetrot', adjective 'globetrotting'. Compare 'jet-setter' (rich, fashionable), 'backpacker', 'cosmopolitan', 'well-travelled'.

en: to spend time and money on luxury and self-indulgence
literal: Middle Dutch pamperen, to cram with food
note: 'Pamper oneself', 'a pampered pet'. Spa marketing: 'a pampering weekend'. Compare 'indulge', 'spoil' (also negative), 'treat oneself', 'cosset' (over-protect).

en: to spend a lot of money freely on something enjoyable
literal: to make a splash with money
note: British informal; 'splash out on a new kitchen'. American equivalent 'splurge'. Compare 'push the boat out' (British, celebrate lavishly), 'treat oneself', 'go to town'.

example.target: We splashed out on a sea-view room for the last night.
example.en: We spent extra on a room with a sea view.

en: a short holiday or escape, especially from routine
note: 'A weekend getaway', 'a romantic getaway'; also 'a getaway car' (escape from a robbery). Compare 'a break' (British: 'a city break'), 'a mini-break', 'an escape'.

example.target: We booked a last-minute getaway to Lisbon.
example.en: We booked a short holiday in Lisbon at short notice.

en: to cook food gently in liquid just below boiling point
literal: imitative of the gentle bubbling sound
note: Cooking verbs: 'simmer', 'poach' (eggs, fish, in liquid), 'braise' (brown then stew), 'sauté' (fry quickly), 'sear' (brown the outside), 'baste', 'blanch'. Figurative: 'simmering anger'.

en: rich, elegant and comfortable; luxurious
literal: a soft fabric with a long pile
note: Informal: 'a plush hotel'. Compare 'posh' (British, upper-class), 'swanky' (informal, showy), 'sumptuous', 'opulent', 'luxurious'. Also 'a plush toy' (US).

example.target: They put us up in a plush suite overlooking the bay.
example.en: They gave us a luxurious room with a view of the bay.

en: heavy and filling in an unpleasant way; also dull
note: British informal; of puddings and pastry; also of dull, heavy writing or people ('a stodgy speech'). Compare 'filling', 'heavy', 'leaden'. Opposite 'light'.

en: to drink alcohol in large quantities, often in a group
literal: German gar aus (trinken), to drink right up
note: Literary or humorous: 'carousing till dawn'. Noun 'carousal'. Compare 'revel' (noisy enjoyment), 'binge', 'booze' (slang), 'make merry' (dated).

en: a day or time when a person stops working to relax
literal: time when a machine is down
note: From computing (system unavailable) to lifestyle: 'I need some downtime'. Compare 'me-time' (informal), 'time off', 'a breather', 'R and R' (rest and recreation, military).

example.target: After the conference I need a week of downtime.
example.en: After the conference I need a week to relax.

en: food that is grown or produced locally and in season
note: Menu-speak: 'locally sourced ingredients', 'farm-to-table' (US), 'seasonal', 'artisan', 'free-range', 'organic'. 'To source' = obtain from a supplier.

en: a person who travels a lot for pleasure, especially to foreign places
literal: a member of the jet set (1950s rich air travellers)
note: Implies wealth and glamour; slightly dated. 'The jet set', 'jet-setting'. Compare 'globetrotter' (neutral), 'frequent flyer' (business), 'tourist' (neutral/pejorative).

en: to eat a meal, especially a large or festive one
literal: Old French disner, to eat (originally breakfast)
note: Formal; 'dine out' (restaurant), 'dine in', 'wine and dine someone' (entertain lavishly), 'dine out on a story' (keep telling it, British). Noun 'diner' (person; US cheap restaurant).

example.target: He's been dining out on that story for years.
example.en: He has been telling that story at dinners for years.

en: a long period of very dry weather with no rain
note: Pronounced DROWT. Figurative: 'a goal drought'. Compare 'dry spell' (short), 'aridity' (permanent dryness), 'water shortage', 'hosepipe ban' (British).

en: extremely cold weather or a bitterly cold period
note: Short and sudden, as opposed to 'a cold spell' (longer). Weather 'snap': also 'a snap election'. Opposite 'a heatwave'. British and American.

example.target: A cold snap in April killed the blossom.
example.en: A sudden cold period in April destroyed the blossom.

en: light rain falling in very fine drops
literal: perhaps Old English dreosan, to fall
note: Noun and verb: 'it's drizzling'. Rain scale: 'drizzle', 'light rain', 'shower' (brief), 'downpour', 'torrential rain', 'deluge'. Cooking: 'drizzle olive oil'.

en: the variety of plant and animal life in a habitat
note: 1980s coinage; now a policy term ('biodiversity loss', 'a biodiversity hotspot'). Compare 'ecosystem', 'habitat', 'flora and fauna' (plants and animals).

en: to make something more resistant to damage, especially by weather
note: Also 'waterproof', 'windproof', 'draught-proof' (British, of houses), 'future-proof' (figurative). Adjective and verb.

en: an area of low-lying land that is flooded or waterlogged
note: Ecological term covering 'marsh' (grassy), 'swamp' (trees), 'bog' (peat, acidic), 'fen' (alkaline, East Anglia), 'mire', 'quagmire' (figurative: a hopeless situation).

en: a gentle, pleasant wind
note: Wind scale: 'breeze', 'gust' (sudden), 'gale', 'storm', 'hurricane' (Atlantic) / 'typhoon' (Pacific) / 'cyclone'. Informal: 'it's a breeze' = very easy; 'to breeze through'.

example.target: A warm breeze came off the sea in the evening.
example.en: A gentle warm wind blew from the sea.

en: the loss of fertile land through drought, deforestation or farming
note: Environmental policy term (UN convention, 1994). Related: 'soil erosion', 'deforestation', 'land degradation', 'overgrazing'. Pronounced de-ZER-ti-fi-KAY-shun.

en: a thick cloud of water droplets near the ground that limits visibility
note: Visibility scale: 'haze' (dust or heat), 'mist' (thin), 'fog' (thick), 'smog' (smoke + fog), 'pea-souper' (dated British, thick yellow fog). Adjective 'foggy'.

en: not harmful to the environment; sustainable
note: Marketing word; 'green', 'sustainable', 'environmentally friendly', 'carbon-neutral', 'low-impact'. 'Greenwashing' = false eco claims.

en: a slight shaking of the ground; a minor earthquake
note: Smaller than an earthquake: 'an earth tremor', 'aftershocks'. Medical: 'a hand tremor'. Compare 'quake' (informal), 'seismic activity', 'the Richter scale'.

example.target: The tremor rattled windows across the city.
example.en: The small earthquake shook windows across the city.

en: the preservation and protection of natural resources
note: 'Wildlife conservation', 'a conservation area' (British: protected townscape). Compare 'preservation' (keeping unchanged), 'rewilding' (restoring nature), 'stewardship'.

en: to melt or become unfrozen after being frozen
note: Intransitive: 'the snow thawed'; transitive: 'thaw the chicken'. Figurative: 'relations thawed'. Compare 'melt' (general), 'defrost' (freezer, food), 'de-ice' (windscreens).

example.target: The pipes burst when the ice began to thaw.
example.en: The pipes burst as the ice melted.

en: uncomfortably hot and humid, of weather or places
note: 'A sweltering afternoon'; verb 'to swelter'. Heat scale: 'warm', 'hot', 'baking', 'sweltering', 'scorching', 'stifling' (airless), 'muggy'/'close' (humid, British).

en: unpleasantly warm and humid, with little air
note: Informal, mostly British. Compare 'humid' (neutral), 'close' (British), 'sticky', 'sultry' (hot and humid, also sexually attractive), 'oppressive'.

example.target: It's too muggy to sleep tonight.
example.en: The air is too warm and humid for sleep.

en: a long, narrow, deep valley cut by a river
note: Compare 'ravine' (narrow, steep), 'canyon' (US, large), 'gully' (small, water-cut), 'chasm' (deep crack), 'glen' (Scottish valley), 'dale' (northern English).

en: the amount of greenhouse gas produced by a person's activities
literal: the footprint of one's carbon use
note: 2000s coinage; 'to reduce / offset one's carbon footprint'. Related: 'carbon offsetting', 'net zero', 'emissions', 'the greenhouse effect'.

en: to search for food or supplies in a natural setting
note: Animals forage; now a fashionable human activity ('foraging for mushrooms'). Compare 'scavenge' (search through rubbish or remains), 'hunt', 'gather', 'rummage' (search untidily).

example.target: We foraged for wild garlic along the riverbank.
example.en: We looked for wild garlic to eat by the river.

en: the top layer of soil, rich in organic matter
note: Agriculture and gardening; 'topsoil erosion'. Related: 'subsoil', 'loam' (ideal mixed soil), 'humus' (decayed matter), 'compost', 'mulch' (protective covering).

en: a sudden flow of water down a slope, usually after heavy rain
literal: a flood that arrives in a flash
note: Compare 'a flood', 'flooding', 'a deluge', 'a torrent' (fast stream), 'run-off' (water flowing over land), 'storm surge' (sea driven by wind).

en: to become less intense or stop, of rain, wind or pressure
note: Intransitive, informal; usually negative: 'the rain never let up'. Noun 'let-up': 'no let-up in the fighting'. Compare 'ease off', 'die down', 'abate' (formal). Irregular: let/let.

example.target: The snow didn't let up for three days.
example.en: The snow kept falling for three days.

en: a hanging spike of ice formed by dripping water freezing
literal: ice + Old English gicel, piece of ice
note: Pronounced EYE-sik-l. Winter vocabulary: 'frost', 'hoar frost' (white crystals), 'black ice' (invisible on roads), 'sleet' (rain and snow), 'slush' (melting snow), 'hail'.

en: to shrink or decrease in amount or strength
literal: Old English dwinan, to waste away
note: Intransitive: 'supplies dwindled', 'dwindling numbers'. Compare 'diminish', 'decline', 'wane' (moon, power), 'peter out', 'ebb away' (tide, strength).

example.target: The fish stocks have dwindled to almost nothing.
example.en: The number of fish has fallen to almost zero.

en: a long period of hot weather, often humid
note: One word or two. Officially defined by meteorological offices (several consecutive hot days). Compare 'a hot spell', 'an Indian summer' (warm autumn), 'the dog days' (hottest part of summer).

en: the natural environment where a plant or animal normally lives
note: 'Habitat loss', 'natural habitat'. Compare 'ecosystem' (the interacting whole), 'niche' (an organism's role), 'range' (geographical spread), 'territory'.

en: a feeling of sickness with an urge to vomit
note: Pronounced NAW-zee-a or NAW-sha. Adjective 'nauseous' (feeling sick, in modern usage) vs 'nauseating' (causing sickness). Verb 'to nauseate'. 'Ad nauseam' = to a sickening degree.

en: to become healthy again after an illness; recover
note: Formal: 'convalescing at home'. Noun 'convalescence', 'a convalescent home'. Compare 'recuperate' (recover strength), 'recover', 'be on the mend' (informal), 'pull through' (survive).

example.target: She convalesced by the sea for a month.
example.en: She spent a month recovering by the sea.

en: a disease that is present in a particular area or group
literal: Greek en + demos, within the people
note: 'Malaria is endemic in the region'; figurative: 'endemic corruption'. Not 'epidemic' (sudden widespread outbreak) or 'pandemic' (worldwide). Also of species: 'endemic to Madagascar'.

en: lasting a long time or recurring often, of an illness
note: Opposite 'acute' (sudden, severe, short). 'Chronic pain', 'chronic shortage'. British informal 'chronic' = very bad: 'the food was chronic'. Adverb 'chronically'.

example.target: He has suffered from chronic back pain for a decade.
example.en: He has had long-term back pain for ten years.

en: a medicine with no active ingredient given to reassure a patient
note: 'The placebo effect', 'placebo-controlled trial'. Plural 'placebos'. Figurative: a measure that only appears to help. Opposite 'nocebo' (harm from expectation).

en: the medical identification of a disease from its symptoms
note: Plural 'diagnoses'. Verb 'to diagnose someone with'. Compare 'prognosis' (predicted outcome), 'a second opinion', 'a misdiagnosis'.

en: the likely course or outcome of a disease
note: 'A good / poor / guarded prognosis'. Plural 'prognoses'. Figurative: 'the economic prognosis'. Verb 'to prognosticate' = forecast (formal, often ironic).

example.target: The prognosis is good if treatment starts early.
example.en: The likely outcome is good with early treatment.

en: relating to a condition that cannot be cured and leads to death
note: 'Terminal illness', 'terminally ill'. Euphemisms: 'life-limiting', 'end-of-life care', 'palliative care' (relieving symptoms, not curing). Also = airport building; computer screen.

en: a sudden attack of illness, especially a stroke or fit
note: Medical: 'an epileptic seizure'. Older 'fit' is informal; 'convulsion' for violent shaking. Legal sense: 'seizure of assets'. Verb 'to seize up' = stop working (engine, muscles).

en: feeling slightly ill, weak or depressed
literal: nautical: a sick sailor was sent below, out of the weather
note: Informal, both British and American; 'I'm a bit under the weather'. Compare 'off colour' (British), 'poorly' (British), 'out of sorts', 'run down' (tired, depleted).

example.target: I've been under the weather all week.
example.en: I have felt slightly ill all week.

en: a medicine or treatment that relieves pain
note: Informal-neutral; medical 'analgesic'. 'Over-the-counter' (no prescription) vs 'prescription' drugs. Related: 'anti-inflammatory', 'sedative', 'anaesthetic' (UK) / 'anesthetic' (US).

en: to make an illness or injury worse
literal: Latin gravis, heavy: to make heavier
note: 'Running aggravated the knee injury'. Also informal 'annoy' ('don't aggravate me'), which purists dislike. Noun 'aggravation'; 'aggravating circumstances' (law) = making a crime worse.

example.target: Cold weather aggravates her asthma.
example.en: Cold weather makes her asthma worse.

en: very thin and weak, usually from illness or hunger
note: Formal, strong: 'emaciated prisoners'. Compare 'gaunt' (thin, haggard face), 'skeletal', 'wasted', 'scrawny' (informal), 'malnourished' (clinical).

en: testing a population for a disease before symptoms appear
note: 'Breast cancer screening', 'a screening programme'. Compare 'check-up' (routine examination), 'test', 'scan', 'early detection', 'a smear test' (British, cervical).

en: to keep a sick person apart to prevent the spread of disease
literal: Italian quaranta giorni, forty days (ships held at Venice)
note: Noun and verb: 'in quarantine', 'to quarantine travellers'. Compare 'isolate', 'self-isolate' (2020 coinage), 'cordon off' (an area), 'lockdown'.

example.target: The crew were quarantined for a fortnight.
example.en: The crew were kept apart for two weeks.

en: a swelling or lump in the body that may be cancerous
note: British 'tumour', US 'tumor'. 'Benign' (harmless) vs 'malignant' (cancerous). Compare 'growth' (informal), 'lump', 'cyst' (fluid-filled), 'lesion'.

en: the time between infection and the first symptoms
note: Epidemiology: 'an incubation period of 5 to 14 days'. Related: 'asymptomatic' (no symptoms), 'contagious' (by contact), 'infectious' (by any route), 'carrier'.

en: redness, heat and swelling in part of the body from injury or infection
literal: Latin inflammare, to set on fire
note: Medical suffix '-itis' = inflammation: tonsillitis, arthritis, bronchitis. Adjective 'inflamed'; 'anti-inflammatory'. 'Inflammatory remarks' = provoking anger.

en: to become unconscious briefly; faint
note: Intransitive, informal. Compare 'faint' (neutral), 'black out', 'keel over', 'swoon' (literary, from emotion), 'collapse'. Also 'pass out' = graduate from a military academy (British).

example.target: He passed out in the heat and came round a minute later.
example.en: He fainted in the heat and regained consciousness after a minute.

en: to recover consciousness after fainting or anaesthesia
literal: to come back round to oneself
note: British 'come round', American 'come to' or 'come around'. Also 'come round to an idea' = be persuaded; 'come round' = visit. Irregular: come/came.

en: the state of being unable to move or feel part of the body
literal: Greek paralyein, to disable at the side
note: Plural 'paralyses'. Adjective 'paralysed' (UK) / 'paralyzed' (US). Figurative: 'analysis paralysis', 'political paralysis'. Verb 'to paralyse'.

en: to become red in the face from heat, emotion or illness
note: 'Flushed with anger / success'. Compare 'blush' (embarrassment only), 'redden', 'go crimson', 'colour up' (British). Also 'flush the toilet', 'a hot flush' (menopause; US 'hot flash').

example.target: She flushed scarlet when her name was read out.
example.en: Her face went red when her name was announced.

en: to breathe with difficulty and a whistling sound
note: Breathing verbs: 'wheeze' (chest), 'gasp' (sudden), 'pant' (after exercise), 'puff', 'snore', 'splutter' (coughing), 'hyperventilate' (over-breathe from panic).

en: a doctor who has specialist training in a branch of medicine
note: British hospital rank (senior specialist); in the US the equivalent is 'attending physician'. Other British terms: 'GP' (family doctor), 'registrar' (trainee specialist), 'locum' (temporary stand-in).

en: an exaggerated worry about one's own health
literal: Greek hypo + chondros, below the breastbone (seat of melancholy)
note: Noun 'a hypochondriac'. Modern medical term 'health anxiety'. Compare 'malingering' (faking illness to avoid work), 'the worried well'.

example.target: His hypochondria kept him in the waiting room every week.
example.en: His obsessive worry about his health sent him to the doctor weekly.

en: to confuse or disconcert someone, usually in a mild way
note: Humorous: 'I was thoroughly discombobulated by the new timetable'. Means confuse or upset. Rare but loved; 'discombobulated' is the common form.

example.target: The time change left everyone slightly discombobulated.
example.en: The clock change left everyone confused.

en: an unimportant, trivial thing
note: Also the dessert, and the adverbial 'a trifle' = slightly ('a trifle annoyed', British, understated). Verb 'to trifle with' = treat lightly: 'not a man to be trifled with'.

en: tending to make choices or changes on impulse; unpredictable
literal: Italian capriccio, a sudden start (perhaps 'hedgehog head')
note: Formal: 'capricious weather', 'an arbitrary and capricious decision' (US legal phrase). Noun 'caprice', 'a whim'. Compare 'fickle', 'mercurial', 'erratic'.

en: to waste time; dawdle
note: Informal, slightly dated and affectionate; 'stop dilly-dallying'. Family of rhyming reduplications: 'shilly-shally' (hesitate), 'hurly-burly', 'willy-nilly', 'helter-skelter'.

example.target: Don't dilly-dally; the bus leaves at six.
example.en: Hurry up; the bus leaves at six.

en: the quality of being too willing to believe things
note: 'It strains credulity' = it is hard to believe. Adjective 'credulous'. Not 'credibility' (believability of a person or story), a very common confusion.

example.target: His excuse stretched credulity to breaking point.
example.en: His excuse was almost impossible to believe.

en: excessively eager to please superiors; grovelling
note: Noun 'sycophant' (pronounced SIK-o-fant). Strong disapproval. Synonyms: 'obsequious', 'fawning', 'toadying', 'bootlicking' (informal), 'brown-nosing' (vulgar).

en: a person who is new to a job or activity; a beginner
note: Formal or literary; originally a new convert. Compare 'novice' (religious, also general), 'tyro', 'rookie' (US sport), 'newbie' (internet), 'greenhorn' (dated US).

en: lasting or recurring for many years; constantly returning
literal: Latin per + annus, through the years
note: Gardening: a plant living several years (vs annual). Figurative: 'a perennial problem / favourite' = recurring every year. Adverb 'perennially'.

example.target: Parking is a perennial complaint at the school.
example.en: Parents complain about parking every year.

en: a feeling of listless boredom and dissatisfaction
note: Pronounced on-WEE. Literary, slightly affected: 'existential ennui'. Compare 'boredom', 'tedium', 'world-weariness', 'listlessness', 'malaise'.

en: to make something less harsh; soften
literal: Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion
note: 'Temper justice with mercy', 'tempered optimism'. Metalwork: 'tempered steel'. Noun 'temper' (anger) is unrelated in feel but same root. Compare 'moderate', 'tone down'.

example.target: The good news was tempered by a warning about costs.
example.en: The good news was softened by a cost warning.

en: a person with a wide range of knowledge and skills
note: Approving: Leonardo da Vinci. Compare 'Renaissance man', 'all-rounder' (British, cricket), 'jack of all trades' (ambiguous: '...master of none').

en: to spend time idly, in a lazy, relaxed way
literal: perhaps imitative of a hanging tongue
note: 'Loll about on the sofa', 'his head lolled'. Compare 'lounge', 'laze', 'sprawl' (limbs spread), 'slouch' (bad posture), 'loaf' (idle, slightly disapproving).

en: the quality of being awkward or clumsy in a social situation
note: Adjective 'gauche' (pronounced gohsh): socially awkward, lacking grace. Also 'gaucherie'. Compare 'maladroit', 'tactless', 'ungainly' (physically clumsy).

example.target: His gaucheness at dinner embarrassed his hosts.
example.en: His social clumsiness at dinner embarrassed the hosts.

en: very tiring and demanding; requiring great effort
literal: to get one's gruel = to be punished (19th-century slang)
note: British 'gruelling', US 'grueling'. Collocates with schedule, journey, match, campaign. Compare 'arduous' (formal), 'punishing', 'back-breaking', 'exhausting'.

en: to talk or write at great length about nothing important
note: British informal: 'stop waffling and get to the point'. Noun 'waffle' = vague talk (also the food, unrelated, Dutch). American near-equivalent: 'to ramble', 'to blather'.

example.target: The candidate waffled for ten minutes without answering.
example.en: The candidate talked vaguely for ten minutes.

en: a secret plan by a group to do something harmful or illegal
note: Pronounced ka-BAL. 'A cabal of ministers'. Compare 'conspiracy', 'clique' (exclusive group), 'faction', 'junta' (military), 'coterie' (select circle, neutral).

en: to become less intense; to calm down
literal: Old French abattre, to beat down
note: Formal, intransitive: 'the storm / pain / enthusiasm abated'. Noun 'abatement' (noise abatement). Compare 'subside', 'die down', 'let up' (informal), 'ease off'.

example.target: The wind abated towards dawn.
example.en: The wind died down near dawn.

en: a state of great disorder, confusion or noise
literal: Milton's 'place of all demons', the capital of Hell
note: Coined in Paradise Lost (1667). 'Pandemonium broke out'. Compare 'bedlam' (from Bethlem hospital), 'mayhem', 'chaos', 'uproar', 'a free-for-all'.

en: a mistake made out of carelessness or ignorance
literal: a mistake that makes you howl (with laughter)
note: British informal: 'a schoolboy howler', 'a translation howler'. Compare 'blunder', 'gaffe' (social), 'faux pas' (French), 'clanger' (British: 'to drop a clanger'), 'boo-boo' (childish).

example.target: The subtitles were full of howlers.
example.en: The subtitles contained many laughable mistakes.

en: lacking in energy and enthusiasm; listless
note: British 'lacklustre', US 'lackluster'. Of performances, results, campaigns. Compare 'uninspired', 'lukewarm', 'mediocre', 'insipid' (flavourless), 'dull'.

en: to think deeply and carefully about something
literal: Latin ruminare, to chew the cud
note: Formal: 'ruminate on/over a problem'. In psychology, 'rumination' = unhealthy repetitive worrying. Compare 'ponder', 'mull over' (informal), 'muse', 'cogitate' (humorous), 'deliberate'.

en: very attentive to the smallest detail; extremely careful
note: Can be praise (careful) or criticism (fussy, hard to please): 'fastidious about hygiene'. Compare 'meticulous' (praise), 'finicky'/'fussy' (criticism), 'punctilious' (formal).

example.target: He is fastidious about how his tea is made.
example.en: He is very particular about his tea.

en: happening by chance in a happy or beneficial way
note: Strictly means 'by chance', not 'lucky', but the 'lucky accident' sense is now standard. Compare 'serendipitous' (happy accident; 'serendipity' is in the starter pack), 'providential', 'fluky' (informal).

en: a false but widely believed idea
note: Logic: 'a logical fallacy' (invalid reasoning); general: 'it's a fallacy that...'. Adjective 'fallacious'. Compare 'misconception', 'myth', 'delusion' (held despite evidence), 'canard'.

example.target: It's a fallacy that lightning never strikes twice.
example.en: The belief that lightning never strikes twice is false.

en: to flatter someone in order to gain favour
note: Always reflexive: 'ingratiate oneself with the boss'. Adjective 'ingratiating' (of a smile, disapproving). Compare 'curry favour', 'suck up to' (informal), 'butter up' (informal).

example.target: He spent the first week ingratiating himself with the partners.
example.en: He spent his first week trying to win the partners' favour.
